News.title: 'Worrying' photos show Regent's Park drought damage after fourth summer heatwave
News.content:
'Worrying' photos show Regent's Park drought damage after fourth summer heatwave

A person in London has shared two photos taken just weeks apart in Regent's Park, and the difference appears stark as the capital's flash drought takes hold amid the fourth heatwave of the summer

View Image People were horrified to see how the drought had affected the iconic Regent's park (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

The UK is experiencing its fourth official heatwave of the summer, with temperatures exceeding 34C on multiple occasions. The country's overall heat record was also beaten twice, with the current temperature record for 2026, which is 37.7C set on June 26 in Lingwood, Norfolk.

‌



While people and animals have been seen struggling in the heat, there's no doubt that nature is also desperate for rainfall, as half of England and the whole of Wales are officially in drought, with July confirmed as the driest month on record. The areas affected not only included the whole of London, but also East Anglia, Hertfordshire, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex – covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and Gloucestershire.

‌



This has lead to several parts of the UK being under hosepipe bans, meaning they're not allowed to use their garden hoses to water plants or field - causing severe damage to UK crops and forcing livestock farmers to rely on winter feed reserves.

‌



While it may be difficult to truly notice the impact of the drought in your everyday life, especially if you live in the middle of a city, one Reddit user decided to compare two photos taken just weeks apart in London's Regent's Park, and it's left others utterly horrified.

"Regent's Park today versus less than two months ago, they wrote on the post as they went on to show the two drastically different photos.

‌



Both photos were taken near the Gloucester Gate entry of the park and were merged to show half of the same area to better highlight the difference.

While the photo captured on 7th June this year showed lush, vibrant green grass with equally verdant trees surrounding it, the shot from 2nd August told an entirely different story.

Rather than green grass, it had turned a parched brown, while the surrounding trees and bushes were drooping from the lack of water and rainfall.

‌



"Damn, we really need a good splash of rain, to help our natural environment," one person said in the comment section.

Someone added: "We were there at the open air theatre yesterday. Huge parts of it aren't even dry grass anymore, it's all been worn away and now it's just dust."

"I miss the rain," another said, to which the poster replied: "Never thought we'd be saying that in London."

‌



UK's record-breaking summer as drought announced

A "flash drought" was declared on July 29 for the whole of London due to the very low rainfall and high temperatures as we are in the middle of the fourth heatwave of the year, the Environment Agency revealed.

The summer of heatwaves first started on 22 May and saw the country's record for the hottest May day broken on consecutive days, forming the western extent of a broader sequence of extreme heat events across Western and Central Europe.

On 25 May, a temperature of 34.8C was recorded at Kew Gardens in London, surpassing the previous record of 32.8C, set in 1922. This was broken again when 35.1C was recorded in the same location the following day. Other records which were broken during the May heatwave included the hottest May day in Guernsey, Jersey, and Wales, as well as the UK's highest May daily minimum temperature

Article continues below

The second heatwave started on 19 June and saw more records broken, including that for the UK's hottest June day when 37.7C was recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June, which marked the fifth-hottest day recorded in UK history.

A third heatwave began on 4 July, with temperatures peaking at 35.5C in Wisley, Surrey, on 9 July. A fourth heatwave began on 28 July, two days after the third heatwave ended, which comes as the Environmental Agency announced a drought. It's also triggered Amber UKHSA heat-health alerts and heightened wildfire risks.

Meanwhile UK weather maps show a four-day heatwave could be right around the corner. The Met Office suggest yet another heatwave will follow in just a few days’ time.

News.title: Nigel Farage – live: Reform UK leader's horrific new 'breaking point' poster is branded 'nonsense'
News.content:
Nigel Farage's Reform UK has proposed using the Royal Navy to transport migrants on the English Channel to France or Belgium under a plan called "operation fortress"

Nigel Farage has been blasted for posting online a new version of his controversial "breaking point" poster.

The Reform UK's latest edit, posted on his X account, depicts migrants at Ceuta rather than Syrian refugees, invoking the 2016 poster denounced by then-Chancellor George Osbourne, who compared it to Nazi propaganda.

Reacting online, other X users voiced their anger. One said: "Talking nonsense again." Another posted: "Desperate deflection and piffle." A third wrote: "Reform is at a laughing point."

Mr Farage, whose MP seat in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, is up for contest next week, debuted the "breaking point" poster on the last week of the 2016 Brexit referendum while serving as UKIP leader.

The new version was posted after Mr Farage, 62, broke his cover at a press conference today to unveil visions to use the Royal Navy to transport migrants on the English Channel to France or Belgium under a plan called "operation fortress". This too has been slammed today.

And, while Mr Farage continues to face mounting pressure over his finances, it has now emerged his deputy, Richard Tice, is under investigation by the standards commissioner over an alleged failure to declare an interest.

Follow live updates below...

News.title: Princess Diana’s wedding dress designer recreates 40-foot veil after it goes missing
News.content:
Princess Diana’s wedding dress designer recreates 40-foot veil after it goes missing

Elizabeth Emanuel, who with her husband, designed the wedding dress worn by Lady Diana Spencer at St Paul’s Cathedral in 1981, has a new challenge

View 3 Images The late Princess Diana on her wedding day 45 years ago (Image: Getty Images)

The designer of Princess Diana’s wedding dress has created a replica of the late princess’s 40-foot veil - more than four decades after the original went missing.

‌



Elizabeth Emanuel has recreated the iconic embroidered veil, which she originally designed with her husband David for Diana’s wedding to the then Prince Charles at St Paul’s Cathedral on July 29, 1981.

‌



In the decades after the royal wedding, Diana’s famous wedding gown has been on display for visitors of both Kensington Palace in London and the late princess’s ancestral home of Althorp House in Northamptonshire, however her veil has always been missing from the exhibits.

‌



Prince Edward shares sweet moment with Prince Louis at Commonwealth Games READ MORE :

Should King Charles join Prince Harry at the Invictus Games? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

View 3 Images Charles and Diana married at St Paul’s Cathedral on July 29 1981 (Image: Getty Images)

Now, Ms Emanuel has been commissioned by Renae Plant, the founder of the Princess Diana Museum, to bring the veil back to life on the 45th anniversary of the royal wedding.

Taking to Instagram, Ms Emanuel shared some unseen photographs of seamstresses and embroiderers working on crafting the original bridal gown in her small studio in Mayfair back in 1981.

‌



She wrote: “Hard to believe it's been 45 years since the royal Wedding! The behind the scenes photos bring back so many memories.”

Speaking to People magazine about the remarkable recreation of the veil, Ms Emanuel explained that adding the accessory to future displays will help ensure the 'whole magic' of Diana's wedding look continues to live on in her memory.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



She told the publication: “'That's why I call it the Veil of Light. You can see the twinkle, and it radiates. The dress isn't as complete without the veil.”

The designer added that once the veil is added to the whole look, the wedding dress “looks lighter, and has this airy, delicate feel to it which you don't necessarily appreciate when you see the dress without all of that. It is an integral part of the design.”

To ensure the new veil is as accurate as possible to the original, Ms Emanuel worked alongside London-based embroidery house Hand & Lock, who produced the first veil in 1981, and has also unearthed the initial measurements they used.

‌



45 years on from the royal wedding, which was watched by 750 million people in 74 countries, Ms Plant is set to take the collection on tour in Autumn, allowing members of the public to catch a rare glimpse of the recreated piece for the first time.

View 3 Images Princess Diana with her wedding dress designers David and Elizabeth Emanuel (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Get)

‌



David and Elizabeth Emanuel went to extraordinary lengths to keep the design of Diana’s iconic wedding gown under wraps until the big day. The pair even destroyed their sketches immediately after showing them to Diana, ensuring they could never end up in the wrong hands. And should the design somehow be leaked, they crafted a second backup dress as a precaution.

David previously told People magazine: "At the time we wanted to make absolutely sure that the dress was a surprise. We didn't try it on Diana. We never even discussed it. We wanted to make sure that we had something there; it was for our own peace of mind, really."

Diana never actually set eyes on the second dress, which was crafted from identical fabric to the first and also featured ruffles around the neck.

News.title: Prince Philip's true personality unearthed in historic school report
News.content:
Prince Philip's true personality unearthed in historic school report

Prince Philip, who was the Duke of Edinburgh, was described as irritable yet a born leader by one of his teachers at Gordonstoun School when he was a boy

View 4 Images Prince Philip joined Gordonstoun in Scotland, and attended the school for five years (Image: Getty Images)

The nature of the late Prince Philip’s personality has been revealed in a recently unearthed school report from when he was a young boy.

‌



Records from the late Duke of Edinburgh's time at Gordonstoun School in northern Scotland have been retrieved, and are now on display in the National Archives at Kew, southwest London.

‌



The documents, which were originally expected to be made public in 2041 but have been put on display much earlier, reveal surprising details about Philip’s teenage years. During his final year at the school in 1938, the school's founder and headteacher, Dr Kurt Hahn, noted an unpredictable temper.

‌



Prince William admits teenage Prince George is embarrassed by him and mum Kate READ MORE :

Should King Charles join Prince Harry at the Invictus Games? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

View 4 Images Prince Philip dressed for the Gordonstoun School's production of 'MacBeth', in Scotland, in 1935 (Image: Hulton Royals Collection)

Despite the bursts of anger that Dr Hahn recommended monitoring so it didn’t become a problem, it was said that Philip was willing to get stuck into "dirty and arduous work".

Writing about the late Queen's husband, Mr Hahn called Phillip a "born leader", but who would need "the exacting demands of a great service to do justice to himself." While Phillip's "best" work was described as "outstanding", his second best "is not good enough".

‌



Despite this, the head of the school - who opened the institution in 1924 and was known for his ‘experimental’ teaching methods - made Phillip school captain at the time because he was "universally liked and respected".

For the same reason, Philip was made captain of the cricket and hockey teams. However, according to the head teacher, the prince’s biggest flaw was his temper. "The lure of the moment remains his danger," he wrote. "He is, at times, too irritable.”

View 4 Images Philip took part in the an inter-schools sports day during his time at Gordonstoun (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

‌



Meanwhile, the school head credited him for having a great "sense of service" for the other students, as well as his "unusual courage and endurance".

The report also read that Philip had a knack for commanding a room, as the document stated: "He has a power of meticulous application, but will only do his best under pressure."

Overall, Philip received an A grade for intelligence and B+ for accuracy, reliability and skill adaptability. His teacher also noted a talent for German speaking, adding that Phillip had a particular interest in Greek military history.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Charles arriving for his first term at Gordonstoun, accompanied by his father, Prince Philip

The report also shows Phillip was a member of Gordonstoun’s Seamanship Guild and went on expeditions to Norway and Scotland.

Article continues below

There, he "proved himself to be a cheerful shipmate and very conscientious in carrying out both major and minor duties. He is thoroughly trustworthy and not afraid of dirty and arduous work."

Gordonstoun is a private institution located in Moray, Scotland, and is known for its strict methods of schooling. King Charles followed in his father’s footsteps as he also attended the school when he was a child from 1962 to 1967.

News.title: British food items at risk due to extreme drought - and what shortages could mean for you
News.content:
British food items at risk due to extreme drought - and what shortages could mean for you

EXCLUSIVE: As shoppers are issued a gloomy warning about potential food shortages amid the prolonged drought, the Mirror takes a look at the issue which has had farmers pleading for help

View 7 Images Farmers have warned that there could be food shortages if action isn't taken (Stock Photo) (Image: ANDY RAIN/EPA/Shutterstock)

With a fourth heatwave and a prolonged drought declared across large parts of the country, Britain's usually proud green lawns have been scorched, while farmers have been left dealing with woeful harvests.

‌



England and Wales have officially recorded their driest July since records began, with southern England having seen its driest month on record, as per provisional statistics from the Met Office. It's now feared this could have worrying knock-on effects for the average supermarket shop, at a time when cash-strapped Brits are already struggling, with rising prices and potential food shortages.

‌



The National Farmers' Union (NFU) has now demanded tax breaks on crucial water storage systems, warning that the country could well face shortages of certain foods. It's a stark warning of how vulnerable our food supply really is in the face of climate change.

‌



UK weather maps show 7C morning chill with 40 areas below 10C – full list READ MORE :

What is causing the prolonged drought?

View 7 Images Dry grass has become a familiar sight across the UK as the drought continues (Image: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock)

Record-low rainfall and relentless temperatures mean that half of England is now facing drought conditions - the third in just five years - leaving millions urged to restrict their water use. This follows four scorching heatwaves in the UK so far this year.

For farmers, it's an uneasy time, and a reminder that we are already very much living through the effects of climate change, with an urgent need to adapt.

‌



Alys Bannister, Campaign Manager for the Sustainable Farming Campaign at Sustain, tells the Mirror: "Effectively, this drought is low rainfall over a prolonged period, multiple heatwaves, that is increasing evaporation, which means soil moisture is drying out. It is climate change that is increasing the likelihood and the severity of this extreme weather."

On top of this, there are the human factors exacerbating the issue. Dr Charlie Taverner, Farming Policy Lead at Food, Farming and Countryside Commission (FFCC) explains: "There are challenges with the lack of investment over decades into water storage and the resilience of our water security, which ultimately feeds into water shortages as well."

Which foods are at risk of shortages?

View 7 Images Vegetables such as cucumbers and leafy greens may be affected (Stock Photo) (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

‌



Alys warns that the types of farming where reliable water sources are vital, from horticulture to livestock, are particularly vulnerable. And Dr Taverner notes that shoppers in the UK aren't used to seeing a direct link between weather and what ends up on our supermarket shelves.

Cereal crops such as wheat and barley may well see reduced yields, with the last five years seeing "disastrous" harvests, given that there is a global market for many such crops, you likely won't see a lack of bread on the shelves anytime soon.

However, there will potentially be a disruption surrounding vegetables which require plenty of water, including cucumbers and leafy greens, with recent upheavals with major suppliers Spain and North Africa illustrating just how reliant we are on other countries for our fruit and veg.

‌



Dr Taverner adds: "We only produce about half of our vegetables, and about a sixth of our fruit, so that it's probably in those areas that we also kind of get affected by global shortages."

Will food prices go up if there are shortages?

View 7 Images Will shoppers notice a difference on their till receipts? (Stock Photo) (Image: PA)

Anna Taylor, Executive Director at the Food Foundation, says we have already seen products such as cocoa spike significantly in price due to climate shocks. Back in January, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported that the price of chocolate had soared by 15 per cent following a relatively stable 25-year period.

‌



One key reason for this is the extremely sensitive cocoa trees, which don't fare well with temperature and rainfall shifts. Poor yields in growing regions in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana resulted in less cocoa being produced, and a hike in the price of raw beans.

These climate shocks, coupled with the conflict unfolding in the Middle East, have led to "a double problem" in terms of food prices and potential shortages. Anna explains: "We're going to be starting to see more and more of these types of shocks hit particular crops and create these inflationary effects and also shortages."

Given that we, as a nation, are highly dependent on imports from countries with more significant water shortages and climate shocks than we are currently seeing, it's more important than ever to become more self-sufficient as a nation, with greater support for the agricultural sector.

‌



According to the British Growers website, Britain is currently less than 60 per cent self-sufficient when it comes to our vegetable & salads supply, a figure that is on the decline, raising concerns as the UK population continues to boom towards some 70 million people.

When could food shortages happen?

View 7 Images In the future, food shortages could become increasingly frequent (Image: ANDY RAIN/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock)

While Dr Taverner doesn't believe we'll see immediate shortages, the risk could become far greater in the years and decades to come should we fail to "grow food in a more climate resilient way", including boosting the all-important production of fruit and veg here in the UK.

‌



He warns: "What we need to be concerned about is the years to come as this becomes more and more normal because we might think we're okay today, but the challenge and the potential shortages could come in years ahead."

What should you do in a food shortage?

View 7 Images Shoppers have been cautioned against 'panic buying' (Stock Photo) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

While this is an issue that goes far beyond individuals, there are things ordinary shoppers can do day to day to limit the impact in their shopping trolley and bank account. Chelsea Kerr, MD of Too Good To Go, UK & Ireland, warns people against "panic buying" in response to potential shortages, instead thinking "creatively" about the ingredients they do have to hand, in a way that helps to cut waste.

‌



The food sustainability expert suggests: "The best thing UK households can do is avoid panic buying and get creative with what they already have at home. At Too Good To Go, we often see people buying ingredients for a single recipe, only for the leftovers to sit unused and eventually go to waste.

"During periods of pressure on supermarket shelves, it's even more important to make the most of the food you already have and embrace flexible, zero-waste cooking using everyday ingredients.

"Not only does this help reduce waste, but it can also make your food shop go further. And of course, consumers can rescue surplus food locally from their favourite brands and retailers, helping communities stretch their budgets while ensuring perfectly good food is eaten rather than wasted."

‌



While the outlook may feel grim, beans, pulses, and legumes tend to remain relatively safe from price rises and can provide essential nutrients for a healthy diet at lower prices, which is why the Food Foundation highly recommends them to low-income households.

Anna pointed towards the Food Foundation's current campaign, Bangin' Some Beans, focused on replacing or supplementing potentially pricey meat products with beans, for example, in "a Bolognese sauce where you might take out a little bit of beef, and you put some beans and lentils in instead."

She enthused: "Delicious on taste, packs loads of punch in fibre, and a much more affordable source of protein. So there are little hacks which savvy shoppers can deploy to try and make that limited budget work in a situation where prices are going up, and meat and dairy have been one of the things where prices really have been going up."

‌



Keeping on top of food waste is also a big one, with Anna urging those with freezers to make use of them to keep budget-friendly leftovers.

What can be done to help farmers?

View 7 Images Scorching conditions have left farmers struggling (Image: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock)

A 10-year weather survey by the NFU last year found that 70 per cent of farmers reported increased heatwaves and heat stress, which made farming more difficult. NFU Deputy President Paul Tompkins last week said that it was becoming "harder, riskier and more costly to produce the nation's food."

‌



Having warned last week that farmers "urgently need secure, reliable access to water", Paul urged: "There are practical steps government and the water supply chain can take now.

"That means creating a risk register for vulnerable farm businesses, improving local communications, being as adaptable as possible with abstraction so farmers can access water when it rains and unlocking the investment and planning changes needed to build more reservoirs. With joined-up government, this can be achieved. Securing water for farming means securing the food on the nation’s plates.”

According to Anna, there's plenty the government can be doing to support farmers forced to adapt to a changing climate, from investing in reservoirs to improve water security, to ensuring greenhouses are afforded the same discounts as other energy-intensive industries receive

‌



Public food procurement, by which public money is used to provide food and catering services in a variety of sectors, will also play a critical role here. As Anna explains: "When the government is essentially buying food for schools, for hospitals, for care homes, and so forth, they could really start to pivot that buying towards more locally, British-sourced food. Lots of opportunity there to build up confidence amongst the farmers that they've got a market for their produce."

Meanwhile, experts at Sustain are dedicated to helping farms transition to what they call "agroecological" or "nature-friendly methods of farming". This would partly involve creating healthier soils that could absorb more water, "like a sponge" during rainfall, which they could then hold onto during drier conditions.

Alys says: "The long-term issue is we really need to make sure that UK food production in the long term remains resilient, we are starting to see climate impacts becoming more severe. If we adapt farming, we are in a better place. We know this extreme weather is going to keep happening, so building adaptation and resilience in our farming means we are more resilient to future shocks. In doing so, that should hopefully bring stability to food prices in the long term."

News.title: Dad and daughter who died in Fistral Beach tragedy identified as family devastated
News.content:
Dad and daughter who died in Fistral Beach tragedy identified as family devastated

John Peter Collins, 66, and his daughter Samantha Adele Collins, 32, both from Doncaster, died after an incident at surfing hotspot Fistral Beach on July 26

View 2 Images The tragic deaths happened at Fistral Beach - one of the UK's most popular surfing areas (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

A father and daughter swept to their deaths at one of Britain's most famous surfing beaches have been named ahead of an inquest opening.

‌



John Peter Collins, 66, and his daughter Samantha Adele Collins, 32, both from Doncaster, were pulled from the water following an incident at Fistral Beach in Newquay - on the night of July 26. Both were pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



Devon and Cornwall Police said the victims' families have been informed and have appealed for information about an orange or peach-coloured handbag belonging to Ms Collins, which is believed to contain personal items of great sentimental value to her loved ones.

‌



View 2 Images Fistral beach in Newquay, Cornwall (file image) (Image: William Dax / SWNS)

Emergency services, including police, coastguard and ambulance crews, were seen at the beach from around 9.30pm into the early hours. Coastguard rescue teams from Newquay, Padstow and St Agnes, alongside Newquay RNLI lifeboats and a HM Coastguard helicopter, assisted with the response, the force said.

An inquest into the deaths of the father and daughter will open on Tuesday and be heard in full at a later date, Cornwall Live reports.

‌



In its latest update on July 27, Devon and Cornwall Police said: "We now understand that the woman who sadly lost her life had entered the water carrying a handbag described as orange or peach in colour, with a shoulder strap.

"The bag is believed to be leather-style and approximately 30cm by 30cm in size. It is thought to contain a number of personal items of great sentimental value to her loved ones.

"At what is an incredibly difficult time for the family, they would take great comfort in being reunited with these belongings if possible. We would be very grateful if anyone who finds a bag matching this description could hand it in to Newquay Police Station or contact us, quoting the incident number 50260197209."

‌



The force has not confirmed whether the bag has since been found.

Following the tragedy, Newquay Town Council said: "We are extremely saddened by the tragic events at Fistral Beach on Sunday evening, in which a father and daughter sadly lost their lives.

"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with their family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time. We would also like to acknowledge the efforts of the emergency services, RNLI volunteers, coastguard teams and all those who responded to the incident."

Article continues below

The council shared the police's appeal for information about the handbag, urging anyone who finds it to contact the force. It also asked people to respect the family's privacy.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Six dead and dozens injured as tourist bus in horror head-on crash in Italy
News.content:
Six dead and dozens injured as tourist bus in horror head-on crash in Italy

A tourist shuttle bus crash crashed in central Italy on Sunday evening, leaving at least six people dead and 34 others injured

View 2 Images A tourist shuttle bus crashed on the Terni-Rieti road in Lazio, central Italy (Image: Vigili del fuoco)

At least six people have been killed and 34 others injured after a tourist shuttle bus crashed in central Italy.

‌



The bus collided head-on with a camper van and two cars on the SS 79 Ternana road, in the province of Rieti in Lazio, on Sunday evening, according to Umbria regional authorities. The incident happened close to the border with Umbria.

‌



Regional president Stefania Proietti said six of those injured were in critical condition, while two others were being treated for serious injuries, according to Italian news agency ANSA.

‌



In an update on Monday afternoon, regional authorities said 15 people remained in hospital and 19 had been discharged. A four-year-old girl was among those receiving treatment, but she was not in a life-threatening condition, Italian newspaper La Nazione reported.

View 2 Images A tourist bus collided head-on with a camper van and two cars on the Terni-Rieti road (Image: Vigili del fuoco)

‌



The privately operated bus was transporting tourists to the Marmore Falls, an ancient Roman waterfall near Terni, Proietti said. She described the crash as a "catastrophic" mass-casualty incident, saying the regional emergency protocol was activated immediately after the first emergency call. The injured were rushed to hospitals in Terni, Perugia, Spoleto, Foligno and Rieti.

Italian media reported that all six people who died in the crash were Italian nationals. Among the victims were bus passengers Paolo Cosci and Graziella Baldini, a couple from the Tuscan town of Massa.

Massa Mayor Francesco Persiani expressed his condolences, writing on Facebook: "In the very serious road accident that occurred along the Terni–Rieti highway, two of our fellow citizens, Paolo Cosci and Graziella Baldini, also lost their lives. It is a deep sorrow that affects our entire community."

Article continues below

According to La Nazione, three other victims were the bus driver, Federico Romualdi, and a couple travelling in a camper van, Giampiero Colasanti and Daniela Bellanca. The identity of the sixth person who died has not yet been released.

News.title: Airbnb guest mortified after discovering what's beneath floor panel in room
News.content:
Airbnb guest mortified after discovering what's beneath floor panel in room

A man staying in an Airbnb felt like he was living in a horror movie after discovering a hidden room beneath the floorboards - and people online were quick to share their thoughts

View Image It caught him off guard (stock) (Image: vintagerobot via Getty Images)

Staying in an Airbnb can throw up all sorts of surprises. It still remains incredibly popular worldwide, featuring roughly 290million estimated users with many guests searching for the perfect rental to create some memories.

‌



Now one man got a little more than he bargained for during a recent stay. The guest was having a look around the property when he came across a chair positioned in a peculiar spot. Since his intrigue got the better of him, he decided to shift the chair to one side which is when he stumbled on quite a big secret and now he can't shake it off.

‌



In a social media post, he showed how he uncovered a red wooden floor panel concealed beneath – hidden under the floorboards.

‌



Unable to resist a peek, he lifted the hatch to find a narrow staircase descending to another closed door below. Posting a video of the find online, he confessed the sight instantly gave him the creeps.

He said: "I rented an Airbnb and noticed there was a chair sitting over what turned out to be a hidden floor panel. I didn't go down there because it didn't feel right." The next morning, the man claimed matters took an even more unsettling turn.

The guest said he believed he heard what sounded like footsteps coming from beneath the floor, though he conceded he couldn't be entirely sure what the noise was.

‌



He continued: "The whole thing just felt really unsettling. What do you think that space is for? And should I go down there because I'm really curious to see what's behind that door?"

The chilling discovery rapidly clocked up thousands of views, with plenty of people drawing comparisons to scenes from well-known horror films.

‌



One viewer quipped: "Various Evil Dead films, Barbarian and The Cabin in the Woods have taught us that you absolutely should go down there and mess with any books, tape recordings and artefacts you find."

Another person commented: "We had a creepy cellar like this at a very old house we rented. The house was built in 1890. So that used to be where they kept 'cold' stuff and jarred stuff and what not.

"It was still freaky as hell. The internet guy went down there and when he came out spiders were leaping off of him."

‌



A third simply asked: "What in the Barbarian did you find yourself in?"

Others took a more pragmatic view, suggesting the concealed space was probably an old cellar or basement that would have been used for storing food, rather than anything more sinister.

While the man didn't specify where the Airbnb was, the company ensures guests alert them immediately if they're in a similar position. The main thing is to not open any hidden doors and to report anything suspicious to them.

‌



Secret rooms

But it turns out he isn't the only one to have uncovered a secret room in a home, as one student discovered a secret room behind a wall in his basement.

He explained how he rented an "old mansion" with some friends while carrying out his studies because the rent was "dirt cheap".

Although the building was "falling apart" around them, they came to love their rented home, living there for more than two years.

Article continues below

The Pittsburgh student called his friends down to the basement before plucking up the courage to peer down in to the room - but nothing could have prepared him for what he saw down there.

News.title: English FA set to withdraw support for Fifa president Infantino
News.content:
The English Football Association is set to write to Fifa president Gianni Infantino withdrawing its support for him amid the fallout from his scrapped plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investors.

It comes as Uefa threatens legal action over the proposals and Wales publicly withdraw backing for Infantino's bid to continue as Fifa president.

Next March, Infantino is set to stand for re-election for a fourth and final term as president and would need 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win.

Sources have told BBC Sport the Scottish FA's position on the future of Infantino remains aligned with Uefa's lack of confidence in the 56-year-old.

Infantino's leadership had already been publicly questioned by football's governing bodies in Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbean, with Uefa and Concacaf releasing statements criticising the plans.

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors would have been able to buy stakes in it.

World football's governing body said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

As first reported by The Telegraph, Uefa said in a letter to Infantino "it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints (together, the 'proceedings') arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by Fifa".

Uefa added it wants "immediate steps" to "preserve all documents and electronically stored information" in Fifa's possession "independent" of their internal policies that may result in "routine document destruction or deletion".

BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced earlier it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties have branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Speaking earlier, Farage said he was "entirely confident" the plan could be justified under international maritime law.

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: Inside city gripped by deadly protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
News.content:
Dozens of people have been killed in clashes between security officials and protesters across Pakistan-administered Kashmir over the last two months, following a crackdown that left the city of Rawalakot mostly sealed off from the world.

Leading the demonstrations is the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which says it is protesting for rights including healthcare and electricity.

Authorities say the JAAC is trying to disrupt the current regional elections, that the group is armed, and will not be allowed to leave Rawalakot.

The JAAC was banned in June; they have been labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the government. They reject this characterisation, saying they are peaceful and - though funded from the Pakistan-administered Kashmir community abroad - not sponsored by India.

The BBC is the first media to gain access to the city and speak to people on the ground about what is going on at the heart of the protests. Pakistan correspondent Caroline Davies reports from Islamabad.

News.title: Son who kept mum's body in freezer for years collected £78k of her benefits
News.content:
A man who kept his dead mother in a chest freezer in the living room of the family home for nearly three years and continued to collect her pension and benefits has been sentenced to two years and four months in prison.

Christopher Phillips, 60, was arrested after the body of Sylvia Phillips, 89, was found by officers in February at Poplar Crescent, Porthcawl, Bridgend county.

She had died in March 2023.

Phillips had told doctors he "did not want to let her go" and "wanted more time" after her death.

Sylvia Phillips was discovered wrapped in a leopard print silk blanket, with yellow and pink roses placed on her body, as well as a birthday card signed from him and the family dog Tina.

"To Mum, from Christopher and Tina," the card read.

Phillips admitted three offences including failing to lawfully and decently bury his mother and continuing to claim her pension and benefits including housing benefits and winter fuel allowances.

Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court heard Phillips had been adopted by Sylvia Phillips at the age of two, was "exceptionally close" to her and was her sole carer.

The day after she died on 8 March 2023 her son held her in his arms and told her he would look after her, the court was told.

Two days after her death, Phillips bought a chest freezer from AO.com, placing it in the dining room of the semi-detached home. She remained there until her body was discovered by police who carried out a welfare check requested by her GP.

The court was told that the local medical practice had made repeated attempts to contact her but were denied access by her son.

When police went to the house, Phillips said his mother had moved to London and did not want to undergo medical tests.

The court heard officers became suspicious, with Phillips seen trembling and fidgeting. He ran upstairs and later could be heard telling a girlfriend on the phone that the "police are going to arrest me, you've got the will".

Officers who opened the freezer found that the 89-year-old was completely frozen and it was some time before a post-mortem was able to be carried out. The pathologist has been unable to ascertain a cause of death, but there were not thought to be suspicious circumstances.

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: X Factor finalist denies murdering influencer by running her over with car
News.content:
A former X Factor finalist has denied murdering a social media influencer by running her over with a car in central London.

Gabrielle Carrington of Manchester, allegedly struck Klaudia Zakrzewska outside Inca nightclub in Argyll Street, Soho, at 04:30 BST on 19 April.

The 29-year-old appeared at the Old Bailey by video link from Bronzefield prison to deny the charge. She had been initially charged with attempted murder but that was changed to murder after Zakrzewska died from her injuries six days later.

Carrington, who was not represented in court by a barrister, also denied a second charge of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to security guard Anoush Chyche.

The defendant was not asked to enter a plea to a third charge of driving with excess alcohol.

Family members of the victims shook their heads as the accused read out her pleas.

Judge Sarah Whitehouse KC confirmed the trial would be held at the same court from 5 January.

Carrington appeared emotional on the video link, wiping tears from her face throughout the hearing and was placed into custody afterwards.

News.title: Threat to oil tankers in Middle East  worst since start of Iran war, analysts say
News.content:
The threat to ships carrying oil in the Middle East is at its worst since the Iran war started, experts have said, after a spate of attacks on another key route in the region.

The warning comes after a number of attacks on vessels in the Red Sea, an alternative waterway that some tankers had been using since Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has denied Donald Trump's claim that it was in talks with the US over reopening the strait, but said it was speaking to Oman about securing the shipping lane.

"In terms of threat to the trade of crude, we're at the worst period that we've been in since this since this crisis began," said Matthew Wright, an analyst at ship-tracking firm Kpler.

The number of ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz was just eight on Sunday and 11 on Saturday, compared with more than 100 per day before the war began, according to Kpler.

Before the conflict, about 20% of the world's oil and gas passed through the strait.

The temporary peace deal with the US struck in early June led to numbers rising again, but the resumption of strikes between the two countries roughly a month later have significantly reduced traffic.

Many ships have been "going dark" when crossing the strait, meaning they turn off their transponder to avoid detection.

For much of the war, some ships carrying oil from Saudi Arabia had instead passed through an alternative shipping lane in the Red Sea, between the kingdom and west Africa.

But a recent spate of attacks by Yemen's Houthi fighters on Saudi tankers using the alternative waterway has further heightened the risks.

News.title: Driest July on record for England and Wales
News.content:
July 2026 was the driest for England and Wales since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, external.

England recorded just 6.5mm of rainfall and Wales had 9.3mm, both less than half of the previous records for the nations.

The dry conditions have been accompanied by exceptional warmth across much of the UK. It was the second warmest July for the UK as a whole and Wales' warmest ever.

The month was also the UK's sunniest July on record. For England and Wales, it was the sunniest calendar month ever observed.

So far this year, six months of 2026 have seen above average sunshine hours for the UK, with just February seeing below the monthly average.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: Presenter Tony Livesey leaves BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years
News.content:
Presenter Tony Livesey has left BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years at the station, the corporation has announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against his former newspaper boss David Sullivan.

He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

Several women have accused Sullivan, a billionaire businessman and West Ham co-owner, of abusing his power and preying on them for sex, in some cases when they were teenagers. Sullivan has strongly denied the allegations.

The claims against Sullivan were made in a joint investigation by the Times and BBC Panorama.

The BBC previously said Livesey had asked to take a break from presenting his programme while the issues raised by the investigation were being examined.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

In an email sent to 5 Live staff on Monday morning, the station's controller Heidi Dawson said he had now decided to leave.

"Tony has asked me to pass on his heartfelt thanks to the brilliant colleagues at 5 Live who he has had the pleasure of working with over the years," she wrote.

"I know many of you have also really enjoyed working with Tony, and we wish him well for all his future endeavours."

The award-winning presenter worked for the BBC from 2006 - the same year he left the newspapers - appearing on 5 Live from 2010 onwards, including a successful stint hosting its drivetime show.

He won radio awards - ARIA and APAs - for his reporting on how it feels to lose your mother as a child, and an ARIAS gold award after he was asked by the late Dame Deborah James to conduct her final interview.

His topical three-hour programme was broadcast on 5 Live from Monday to Thursday, featuring interviews and phone calls from listeners.

News.title: Grooming gang found guilty of exploiting teenage girls for sex
News.content:
Four men and a woman have been found guilty of being part of a grooming gang that exploited teenage girls for sex.

Mustafa Iqbal, Mohamed Arshad, Ziaullah Badshah, Jaswinder Singh were convicted of conspiracy to traffic their victims, who were aged 14,15 and 16.

At Caernarfon Crown Court on Monday, Iqbal, Arshad and Badshah were also found guilty of rape while another member of the gang, Sarah Gray, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice and assisting an offender.

The men were remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on 25 September, while Gray was released on bail.

Prosecutor Owen Edwards KC said the men had used the three girls - named only as Child A, B and C - like "sexual commodities".

"They took full sexual advantage of Girl B in particular," he said.

The jury was told Child A had been treated as a "sexual plaything", who finally had gone to the police after having been handcuffed by Iqbal and had been raped.

The court heard the teenagers were given drugs and sexually abused in cars, homes and businesses in Rhyl, Denbighshire and the surrounding area between April 2022 and March 2024.

The first two victims, Child B who was 15 and Child C who was 14, were approached by Iqbal, 43, near a petrol station in the town, and he persuaded them to come back to his home.

They were later joined by local coffee shop owner Arshad, 36, and his friend Badshah, 25.

During the trial the jury had been told how the two girls stated they were 17, had smoked cannabis with the men and had played a game of spin the bottle.

Badshah, who came to Rhyl as a refugee from Pakistan when he was 15, admitted kissing Child B and Child C, and on later occasions having sex with Child B at his home.

Badshah, of Brighton Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, supplying cannabis to another.

Arshad, 36, of Clifton Grove, Rhyl, was found guilty of three counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, and supplying cannabis to another.

The court heard one of the counts of rape happened in an alleyway outside his former business, Zayn's Coffee House.

Iqbal, of Trellewelyn Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of raping Child B and also sexually assaulting Child C. He was also found guilty of raping another teenager, Child A, who was 16 and lived in a care home.

Described as a drug dealer during the trial, he supplied Child A with crack cocaine and cannabis in return for sex.

Iqbal was convicted of 21 offences, including four of rape and three of sexual assault. He was also found guilty of conspiracy to traffic and conspiracy to supply cannabis and cocaine, breaching a trafficking risk order, and he pleaded guilty to possessing a prohibited weapon.

The gang was unmasked after another friend of the men took Child B to London.

Former builder Singh, 61, claimed the girl was looking after his dog and there was no sexual motive in taking her on the trip to see his family in the capital, but a concerned adult was alarmed by Singh's intentions and reported him to the police.

Singh, of River Street, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of conspiracy to traffic and one count of supplying cannabis to another.

Gray, 53, of Llanasa Road, Gronant, was also found guilty of conspiracy to supply cocaine to another and conspiracy to supply cannabis to another.

After the guilty verdicts Det Ch Insp Richard Sidney said his thoughts were the three young victims.

"They were children, aged just 14 to 16, when they were subjected to exploitation and abuse by adults who took advantage of their vulnerabilities and sought to manipulate and control them for their own gain," he said.

"No child should have to experience what these young women endured."

He said that the five defendants had denied almost every allegation against them from the outset.

"I hope today's outcome sends a clear message that those who seek to groom and exploit vulnerable children will be relentlessly pursued," he said.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line

News.title: Comedian Jimmy Cricket dies aged 80
News.content:
Comedian Jimmy Cricket has died aged 80 after a short illness, his family said.

In a statement posted to social media they said Cricket spent his last few days surrounded by his family, love, laughter and songs.

"Forever our clown, he was cracking jokes to the wonderful NHS staff and to us all, right until the end. His courage, dignity and positivity through all he endured was inspirational," they added.

The comedian, from Northern Ireland, became a household name in the 1970s.

Born in Cookstown, County Tyrone in 1945, Cricket left school at 16 and started the summer season of 1966 as a Redcoat for Butlins.

He worked the comedy club scene in the 1970s and 1980s, going on to win LWT's Search for a Star talent contest and eventually getting his own TV show on ITV and a radio series on BBC Radio 2.

Cricket's family said he had been a "force for joy" and the world was a "far less sillier place today".

"We were going to end by using his famous catchphrase and say: 'There's no More'.

"But Jimmy was a man of great faith and a Papal Knight of the Catholic Church.

"He believed that death is not the end and was looking forward to eternity, so reallyâ¦ And there's more."

News.title: I didn't know I'd been hosting a parasite for years - until the most intense pain of my life
News.content:
Jones remembers the May 2016 night when he went into hospital â he was supposed to go out to a dinner with his wife Eileen, but he stayed at home as he felt unwell.

"I hadn't been able to control the pain, and it was more intense than anything I had before.

"Then about midnight, we had to call the ambulance, and they took me to Nevill Hall. Whatever they gave me there cured the pain. I haven't experienced pain like that before."

Jones was in hospital for 10 days, and says the doctors there suspected he had hydatid cysts immediately.

He said: "There was a lot of it around this area at the time, and I remember the Ministry of Agriculture giving worming treatment to the dogs on the local farms.

"Whether they could see that I was an old sheep farmer or not, that might have had a bearing on it. We had plenty of experience in this area â Breconshire as a whole â of hydatid cysts, people that have suffered through it, numerous examples."

Jones was then referred to "the main expert on hydatid cysts" in London where he had two operations in 2018 and 2019 to remove them, one from each lung.

"I swapped two cysts for two scars on the ribs," he said, adding that he still has a cyst on his liver, which surgeons decided not to remove.

News.title: Scottish islanders refused permission to stage annual seabird chicks hunt
News.content:
Permission has been refused for a guga hunt which would have seen hundreds of young seabirds killed on an uninhabited Hebridean island.

For centuries, gannet chicks have been hunted for their meat each summer on Sula Sgeir, a small rocky island 40 miles (64km) north of Ness on Lewis.

Modern hunts require a licence from public agency NatureScot, which rejected the application this year due to concerns about the impact on the gannet population.

Animal welfare groups have welcomed the decision, but supporters accused campaigners of "bullying" a small island community.

The decision to refuse a licence for Scotland's last remaining guga hunt this year was taken by NatureScot's board following a recommendation by officials.

News.title: Glasgow hailed for saving Games as baton passes to Amdavad
News.content:
The man responsible for delivering Glasgow 2026 said the city had "saved and reinvented" the Commonwealth Games, three years after its future was plunged into doubt.

Ahead of Sunday's closing ceremony - which featured a dazzling fireworks display over the River Clyde - Phil Batty recalled how Glasgow stepped up when the original hosts pulled out.

And he believes the legacy of the sustainable, scaled-back Games will shape the future of the multi-sports event.

The Commonwealth flag has been handed over to the Indian city of Amdavad, also known as Ahmedabad, which will stage the centenary event in 2030.

But Batty said Glasgow's decision to host the event for a second time in 12 years would never be forgotten.

He told BBC Scotland News: "We have created a Games here that will inspire more nations to host but, probably more importantly, that every nation feels it could host at some point in the next 100 years."

News.title: Almost £200,000 of fuel stolen from UK forecourts every day since Iran war began
News.content:
UK drivers have stolen almost Â£200,000 of fuel from petrol stations on average every day since the Iran war broke out and sent prices soaring, according to industry analysis.

Incidents of fuel being taken from forecourts without payment have risen by a fifth in the five months since 28 February, figures from Forecourt Eye suggest.

The conflict in the Middle East severely disrupted oil supplies across the region, triggering a rise in wholesale prices and subsequent increase in costs at the pump in the UK.

Forecourt Eye said the value of the stolen fuel is estimated to have risen by 48% compared with the five months before the war - to reach an estimated daily average of Â£194,000.

The fuel theft prevention company added petrol stations are reporting an increase in "abuse, intimidation and violence from frustrated customers".

The figures are based on a representative sample of 550 forecourts, comparing the five months prior to the outbreak with the five months after it started, and extrapolated to the UK's 8,359 forecourts.

The number of incidents recorded at the forecourts in the sample equates to 2,872 daily incidents on average at forecourts across the UK in the months after war began, up from around 2,400.

They include people driving off without an attempt to pay, and people claiming they have no way to pay after filling their vehicle.

The volume of stolen fuel rose by 24% - up from an estimated 87,000 litres to 108,900 litres a day across all forecourts.

In response, Forecourt Eye said it would partner with facial recognition company Facewatch to offer more than 2,000 retailers free access to crime reporting technology from the autumn.

Southern England saw not only its driest July but also its driest month ever recorded, amid what the Met Office called one of the “most notable summer months” since records began.

Forecasters said last month was a double-record breaker for both England and Wales, with both nations experiencing their sunniest July since data began as well as their driest.

It comes amid a summer of extreme heat and dry weather across the country which has seen back to back heatwaves and left all of Wales and half of England plunged into drought.

Farmers have warned the exceptionally dry conditions could lead to food shortages later in the year, as the Met Office said increasingly extreme conditions are becoming the new norm.

New data from the forecaster shows just 1.9mm rain was measured across Southern England last month, narrowly beating the previous record low of 2.0mm in February 1891. It was also the driest July for England and Wales since records began in 1836, according to provisional figures released.

England saw just 6.5mm of rain across July, or 10 per cent of the long-term average for the month, less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

Wales had 9.3mm of rainfall, or 9 per cent of the average, again well below the previous record of 22.6mm set in 1911. Northern Ireland saw its eighth driest July, with 26.9mm of rain, the equivalent of 30 per cent the average for the month.

Scotland was the only nation not to trouble the record books last month, with 69 per cent of its average rainfall.

The UK as a whole experienced its third driest July, with 28.9mm of rain: the lowest figure for the month since 1868.

UK peak daily temperatures in 2026 ( PA Wire )

England clocked up 305.6 hours of sunshine across the month, surpassing the previous July record of 294.8 hours set in 1911, while Wales saw 308.0 hours, beating the previous record of 297.5 hours in 1955.

Met Office sunshine data begins in 1910.

Wales also equalled its record for the highest mean temperature across the month, at 17.8C, matching the figure reached in 2006.

England saw its second warmest July on record, with a mean temperature of 19.2C, just below the record of 19.3C set in 2006.

Met Office temperature data starts in 1884.

News.content:

Employees in customer service industries often face hostility in their work environments. When interacting with the public, customers can be rude or demanding.

In recent years, the public has grown increasingly toxic and sometimes dangerous. If a customer yells or threatens an employee, that interaction on its own is jarring. But when these incidents accumulate over months and years, the mental health toll grows.

Our recent research found there are tactics individual employees can use to improve their own work experience.

The study — co-authored with research psychologist William P. Jimenez of the U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences — focused on taxi drivers, who are often on the front lines of customer interactions, work long hours and perform a great deal of emotional labour.

open image in gallery Employees in customer service industries often face hostility in their work environments ( Getty/iStock )

Difficult customers take a toll

As people become exhausted with their jobs, burnout rates can skyrocket with no relief in sight.

Across studies of customer-facing employees, we have found that difficult customer interactions increase burnout, elicit rule-breaking behaviours and influence whether workers want to remain in their occupation.

Employees have little recourse to improve their situations. Those working in customer service industries are especially vulnerable because the workforce is disproportionately made up of young people, women, racialized workers and people in precarious socioeconomic positions.

Compared with workers who hold greater social and economic power, they may have fewer alternative employment options and less ability to challenge unfair treatment. Because they depend on these jobs, they may feel compelled to tolerate conditions that more privileged workers could afford to leave.

Responsibility for fixing this sits clearly with employers, who have tools such as customer conduct policies and managerial support to reduce how often these situations happen. What we studied is whether, in the event a difficult interaction happens anyway, an employee can do something in the moment.

We tend to forget the good things

In our study, we adapted a “three good things” intervention that had employees engage in a positive work reflection looking back at three positive events from their day, to see how this impacts their behaviour at work (one of the only things they can control).

As people, we tend to forget the positive things that happened to us throughout our day, ruminating instead on things that went wrong or situations that upset us. These instances evoke stronger and more immediate physiological, cognitive and behavioural responses.

But this means it’s also something we can intervene to correct. What we focus on determines much of how we feel, so if we choose to look back on our workday searching for instances of goodness and reflecting on what we like about our jobs, we’re more likely to feel better about the work we do and we will, in turn, feel more satisfaction and do better at it.

By focusing on three good things, we found that small, specific occurrences were the best way to prompt people to think differently about their workday. These could be as small as making progress towards a goal, receiving positive feedback, being offered a new opportunity or having a pleasant interaction.

In reflecting on instances like these, employees in customer-facing industries were empowered to process positive experiences more fully. These reflections can change how people feel about their workday, which in turn influences how they behave at work. If people feel better about their jobs, they do better at them.

What our study found

We found that taxi drivers who naturally focus on opportunities, growth and achieving their goals had more success with the intervention overall.

Reflecting on positive experiences increased employees’ positive emotions and significantly increased their extra-role service behaviour, while reducing rule-breaking behaviours. Drivers went above and beyond to ensure a positive experience for customers, and avoided actions that could impede that experience, like driving aggressively.

The intervention also enhanced employees’ active responses to unreasonable demands from entitled customers. They were better able to understand the reasoning behind a demand, explain why accommodating it was impossible, or express understanding of a customer’s frustration.

Because customer-facing employees often have limited control over how customers behave, interventions like this focus on one thing employees can control: how they process and reflect on their work experiences.

A tool for employees and managers alike

While organizations are increasingly implementing measures to encourage respectful customer behaviour, this kind of individual reflection isn’t a replacement for that structural work. It’s something workers can do in the meantime, while broader protections catch up.

Our findings suggest that taking a few minutes at the end of the workday to reflect on three positive experiences is one simple, evidence-based way to do so.

Su Kyung (Irene) KimAssistant Professor, Asper School of Business, University of Manitoba. Xiang Yao is an Associate Professor, Department of Management and Social Psychology, Peking University. Xiaoxiao Hu is a Professor of Management, West Virginia University. Yujie Zhan is a Professor of Organizational Behaviour and Human Resource Management, Wilfrid Laurier University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Our research focuses on a bottom-up approach, in which employees take the initiative, but the deeper fix has to come from employers: setting clear boundaries with abusive customers, staffing shifts adequately and stepping in when interactions turn hostile.

A reflection exercise can help someone get through a bad day. It can’t substitute for a workplace that works harder to prevent bad days in the first place.

Andy Burnham’s first two weeks as prime minister have been marked by a flurry of policy announcements, as the former mayor has looked to mark a clear departure from his predecessor.

It has been successful opening according to the leader’s approval ratings, which have skyrocketed since he entered Number 10. Mr Burnham now sits at a net 19 point approval rating, according to a recent More in Common poll, higher than Sir Keir Starmer achieved at any point in office.

Writing as he reached a fortnight in power, Mr Burnham said his government will have a “clear political direction, rooted in the values [the Labour] movement was built on.”

“I’m not going to be shy about it: this is the start of a complete rewiring of economic and political power in Britain,” he wrote for LabourList.

open image in gallery Speaking to his new cabinet for the first time, Mr Burnham told them they his will be a “cost of living government” ( PA Wire )

Initially focusing on the cost of living, the early policy pledges have now spanned to education, social care, immigration and more.

More detail on many of the announcements can be expected from chancellor John Healey’s first Budget, confirmed to be taking place on 28 October. This is when he will lay out the crucial details on how the funding will be raised for the plans, which experts have warned could spell tax rises to come.

Here are the policies that have been confirmed by the Burnham government so far:

Energy bill VAT cut

One of Mr Burnham’s first moves was to scrap VAT on household electricity bills from October, expected to cut £45 from the average household’s energy bills.

The Treasury said the VAT cut would cost around £850m this financial year and would be funded by cancelling the government’s planned Digital ID programme.

However, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) highlighted in November that the cost of the Digital ID scheme was “unfunded”, as it was based on savings from departmental budgets not yet identified.

Mr Burnham also said that he is looking at energy bill standing charges and water bills in an interview with The Mirror at the start of August.

Bus fares capped

The £2 bus fare cap has been reinstated, Mr Burnham announced on the third day of his premiership, reversing the decision to increase it by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Reinstating this maximum fare will partly be funded by switching grants for international climate projects to repayable loans instead.

The cost of train travel may be Mr Burnham’s next target, as he told The Mirror on Sunday: “I think rail fares are too high, outrageously so in some instances. So that's something that's in my sights.”

A plan to end rough sleeping

Mr Burnham used his inaugural speech to say that his “first instruction” will be to “end rough sleeping in our country.”

In further details set out by Number 10, £340 million funding was announced to go towards acquiring suitable homes, identifying those most in need and starting to provide housing and support “without delay”.

The funding will provide 1,200 homes and intensive support for at least 3,000 long-term rough sleepers over a five-year period, the government said.

Number 10 North

One of Mr Burnham’s flagship proposals is the creation of an outpost of Downing Street based in Manchester, dubbed “No 10 in the North”.

Heron House, an existing government building partially occupied by GCHQ, is serving as the interim headquarters with Mr Burnham vowing to work from the location one day a week.

Business rates rebalanced

Business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues in England will be cut by 20 per cent, Mr Burnham has announced, delivering on a pledge he made on the campaign trail.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey at the Hare pub in Harlow, Essex (Richard Pohle/The Times/PA) ( PA Wire )

The new rates will take effect from April, saving the typical pub an estimated £1,100 according to the government.

The £100m package will be fully funded, it adds. This will be partly through a review of reliefs for businesses that “do not make a positive contribution to local communities”, such as vape shops.

Tax sharing for mayors

Metro mayors across England will be granted new powers to retain a portion of locally raised tax revenue under fresh devolution plans.

Mr Burnham confirmed the policy during a visit to Leeds, stating that regions need “true financial autonomy, not just hand-outs from Westminster.”

The policy will allow more mayors to keep a portion of business rates raised in their area from spring, and eventually a percentage of income tax raised locally.

Education overhaul

Mr Burnham has announced a major shake-up to the education system, designed to rebalance its focus away from university and towards technical qualifications.

Under the plans, students will have the option to combine core academic subjects like English, maths and science, with technical education linked to jobs available in their area.

open image in gallery Mr Burnham has promised a sweeping reform of the social care system ( Getty )

This route will be available from age 14, in Year 10. Students taking this pathway will also spend time with employers to gain work experience.

Social care reforms

Mr Burnham has promised a sweeping reform of the social care system, vowing to immediately begin empowering the work force by integrating staff with the NHS to boost pay and security.

The prime minister also announced that he would expedite Baroness Louise Casey’s commission into social care, bringing its deadline forward from 2028 to next year.

Tackling small boat crossing

The prime minister has pledged that the government will be “relentless” in lowering the number of people arriving to the UK on small boats.

His comments came as he backed new Home Office statistics that show that the number of National Crime Agency (NCA) officers who tackle smuggling gangs enabling small boat crossings has risen to almost 800 from 376 at the start of last year – a new record.

Nuclear renewal

On defence, Mr Burnham has announced a £8.4bn investment in the UK’s nuclear deterrent in the fourth phase of the UK’s Dreadnought Class submarine programme.

The Ministry of Defence has said this will boost the number of jobs on its nuclear programme from 47,000 to 65,000 by 2030, including 20,000 apprenticeships by 2035.

News.title: Vampire fanatic detained after dumping dead deers and lambs outside New Forest churches
News.content:
