In the 2018-19 season, Como were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football, after going bankrupt twice in the previous 15 years. Last season, the small northern Italian club finished fourth after an extraordinary campaign, producing a series of outstanding performances that surprised the football world.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Scrapped proposals, statement wars and the ongoing Infantino furore
Sports.content:
ANOTHER LONG WEEKEND

Here we go again. And, no, we are not talking about the start of the new Scottish Premiership season or the preliminary round of the Carabao Cup – although that Tranmere v Rochdale shootout was a cracker. Yes, after a week of talk about money, greed and Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s brother, the hot topic around the water cooler on Monday was again Gianni Infantino and, more specifically, the English and Welsh FAs’ decisions to row back on their support of a stalling ship. Along with Finland, they’re the first of Uefa’s 55 members to withdraw their letters of support for next year’s Fifa overlord elections.

By the time Football Daily hits your inboxes, there could be a flurry of other nations frantically clicking unsend on those endorsement emails – more than 200 had their flags planted on Terra Gianni just a matter of weeks ago. This U-turn has us harking back to the hazy days of the €uropean $uper £eague, when the Premier League’s super-elite turned their backs on the super-project one by one. Instead of a handful of club statements and Petr Cech trying to calm protestors on Kings Road, now we could be looking at hundreds of withdrawals from federations across the world. Who will go next? Norway? Japan? Would Gianni pick up the phone to the Oval Office if US Soccer decides enough is enough, maybe to try and get it to reverse the decision? Or at least suspend it until next year.

Either way, the threat of a World Cup boycott is over – for now – after Fifa scrapped its proposal to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors in the early hours of Saturday morning. It was half past midnight in the UK when a statement “attributable to the Fifa president” appeared on its website. That followed a statement called “Clarifications on Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE)” at 4am the night before that doubled down on the plans. It’s not exactly reassuring that such major dealings and decisions are being pondered, seemingly by one man, in the dead of night – but then again, these could be learned behaviours after all.

Statement wars continued with Uefa’s response on Saturday morning, which read: “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game.” That dubious is doing a lot of work there. Uefa added: “The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family.” The first member of the football family out of the traps on Monday morning – once it had given the Cymru Premier’s opening weekend time in the spotlight – was the Welsh FA. It withdrew that precious letter of support for Gianni and proclaimed: “Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.” Football Daily waits with bated breath to find out what the next statement will say. The Premier League, after all, is still three weeks away.

RECOMMENDED LOOKING

It’s the 50th anniversary of the first ever Panenka penalty so here is a labour of love/splendid piece of work remembering 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip since 1976.

View image in fullscreen The classic. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Some worried about health problems or being unable to attend because of bad weather, as well as people who frequently travel for work. They are terrified and all asking the same question: will our season tickets be taken away?” – La Provincia, Como’s local paper, says it has received dozens of calls and emails from concerned supporters after the club said it will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules.

double quotation mark I write to you with my deep regret on hearing about the death of the heroic and granite-made Franco Baresi. Two moments stand out to me, both off the pitch, and show what a great man he was. The first was when Arrigo Sacchi, the Milan manager, dropped his intensity in training, fearing he was overworking the players; Baresi convinced Sacchi to up it instead for the sake of the team, with spectacular results. The second was an older Baresi reflecting on his 1994 World Cup final loss to Brazil, which he appeared in 25 days after knee surgery. Rather than lamenting his lot, having missed a penalty and lost the final, Baresi instead recalled watching the 1970 final between Italy and Brazil, only the second game he had seen on TV. The first game was the West Germany v Italy semi-final, where he recalled watching the players who ‘to me, they were Martians’. He said: ‘I would never have thought 24 years later, at 34 years old, I would have the possibility to play in that same game, the final, against Brazil, the same team. It was a dream that came true.’ Rest in peace” – Nick Kinsella.

double quotation mark I was wondering if Gianni Infantino might revist his Big Sale Opportunity by allowing smaller, club-level contestants from less lucrative leagues to participate in a seriously revamped World Cup, replacing their boycotting national sides. For instance, from the lower leagues of Scottish competitions. Mainly to render possible the wonderful hypothetical headline result of the last match of the (?) 2038 edition: Fifa Forward Final fiasco … East Fife 4, Forfar 5” – Russell Richardson.

double quotation mark Steve Bennett’s comment on Newcastle United’s new kit (Friday’s Football Daily letters) made me think of West Bromwich Albion’s similarly ‘bar-coded’ Premier League strip from the 2020-21 season, at the end of which they were relegated. Newcastle may have to hope that isn’t an omen” – Derrick Cameron.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Russell Richardson. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time
Sports.content:
It is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Totti dusted it off for the internet generation at Euro 2000.

It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means. The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.

A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder. Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards, asked the man himself what constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible. Rob Smyth

View image in fullscreen The man himself, pictured earlier this year. Photograph: Björn Steinz/The Guardian

Antonin Panenka, 1976

Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)

This one needs no introduction. RS

Antonin Panenka, 1979

Czechoslovakia 2-0 France

The next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsy with a sensual chip in a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80. RS

Diego Maradona, 1984

Napoli training

Most of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner to ensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d already seen him do it in open play. RS

Eric Cantona, 1989

Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)

In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackle of comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowd and tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot, he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset. Daniel Harris

Gianluca Vialli, 1990

Monaco 2-2 Sampdoria

In the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure: against Genoa in the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90. The first was against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16, the second in the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0 in the final. RS

Michal Bilek, 1990

Czechoslovakia 5-1 USA

It’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976. He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!” RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

Nottingham Forest 1-1 Tottenham

Nobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led to a brief post-match discussion in which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. This one was particularly sweet – the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final. RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

England 1-1 Brazil

A kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearer chuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak, as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record. Jonathan Liew

View image in fullscreen With a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos. Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

Eric Cantona, 1994

Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)

In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final, he’d gently rolled two penalties into the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the way only for the kick to sail over the bar as United lost 6-5. DH

Djalminha, 1995

Guarani 2-1 Internacional

Brazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for his signature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot. The first of many was scored against Sergio Goycoechea, whose elastic penalty saves had taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1996

Sheffield United 0-1 Aston Villa

Dwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule, but Yorke was true to his word and settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.” RS

Gianluca Vialli, 1996

Chelsea 2-4 Wimbledon

There’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. But Vialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line by a very different kind of chip earlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1998

Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal

“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman, who was Panenka-ed on the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called, Yorke sidefooted wide. RS

John Eyre, 1999

Torquay 0-1 Hull City

If only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue as this piece of effrontery floated gently past him. RS

Francesco Totti, 2000

Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)

In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti, whose falling leaf penalty foxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation. John Brewin

View image in fullscreen Francesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century. Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty Images

Mixu Paatelainen, 2001

Hibernian 0-0 Hearts

A last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares. Mixu Paatelainen only took it because Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion. RS

Thierry Henry, 2003

Arsenal 3-2 Newcastle

Five days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner was teased softly down the middle by Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was just trolling Ruud van Nistelrooy. RS

View image in fullscreen Thierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle. Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images

Mickaël Landreau, 2004

Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)

For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka. Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup. Jeff Rueter

Liam Lawrence, 2004

Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)

Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). On the Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.

double quotation mark LL I’m gonna dink it. BH No you’re not. LL I am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final. BH Liam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.

He dinked that ball against the bar – “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.” RS

Helder Postiga, 2004

Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)

Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty, a kick so under-amped it barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp. JB

Peter Crouch, 2006

England 6-0 Jamaica

The then-Liverpool striker scored an England hat-trick as part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ball well over the bar from 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.” Will Unwin

View image in fullscreen Judging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Artem Milevskiy, 2006

Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)

You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it came after 120 minutes of the most soporific football ever played. RS

Zinedine Zidane, 2006

Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)

The nerve to do it in a World Cup final. The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar, past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – until Marco Materazzi and the anger took over. Taha Hashim

View image in fullscreen Zinedine Zidane steps up… Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen … and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA Images

Yann Kermogant, 2010

Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)

To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier, dollied his kick into the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even has his own Bonnie Tyler adaptation. JB

Sebastián Abreu, 2010

Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)

If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one of the first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup. A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions. RS

Andrea Pirlo, 2012

England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)

When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ball wafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successes finishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards. DH

View image in fullscreen Andrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart. Illustration: Matthias Schräder/AP

Sergio Ramos, 2012

Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)

For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-final against Portugal. Bruno Alves missed Portugal’s next kick and Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final. RS

Maicosuel, 2012

Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)

The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenka was saved in a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.” RS

Graziano Pellè, 2012

SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)

Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpah to try a Pellènka? RS

Rogério Ceni, 2013

São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)

No surprise that one of the great goalscoring keepers should beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he was fractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically. RS

Alexandre Pato, 2013

Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)

Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to take one of the worst Panenkas ever seen. RS

Alexis Sánchez, 2015

Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)

It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone. His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – and unlike Czechoslovakia in 1976, they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria. RS

Aaron Ramsey, 2017

Serbia 1-1 Wales

The Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramsey unwittingly did so by scoring a Panenka at the same end of the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one. RS

View image in fullscreen Aaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

George Calintaru, 2017

Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua Bucuresti

A Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger. RS

Fedor Smolov, 2018

Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)

Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend that Fedor Smolov’s opening attempt lacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour. JR

Lionel Messi, 2020

Barcelona 2-2 Atlético Madrid

If you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium, you might as well do it in style. RS

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

Fara Williams, 2020

Reading 3-1 Aston Villa

This unusual penalty from Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority. RS

Ademola Lookman, 2020

West Ham 1-0 Fulham

During his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the game but his feeble chip landed straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare moment of post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.” Yara El-Shaboury

Santi Cazorla, 2021

Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al Sadd

Not many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right foot against Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021. RS

Sergio Agüero, 2021

Man City 1-2 Chelsea

City were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided to chip down the middle; Édouard Mendy almost fell for it but had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüero issued a public apology. WU

View image in fullscreen Sergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty Images

Marta, 2022

France 2-1 Brazil

Birthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against France in sublime fashion.JR

Karim Benzema, 2022

Manchester City 4-3 Real Madrid

A moment of mischief at the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final. RS

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Achraf Hakimi, 2022

Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)

If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final, you might as well do it in style. RS

Gaëtane Thiney, 2023

Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FC

We can’t say for sure that this is the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition. RS

Antoine Mille, 2024

Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)

In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after saving one of the more pitiful Panenkas ever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille. RS

Marta, 2025

Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego Wave

If you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025, chipping in off the underside of the crossbar to secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill. Tom Garry

Alexia Putellas, 2025

Roma 0-4 Barcelona

Even the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenka harmlessly over the crossbar during a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner. TG

Tiaguinho, 2025

Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)

A Panenka is a dish best served cold. RS

Brahim Díaz, 2026

Morocco 3-0* Senegal

Brahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenka was easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding. Then again … YE-S

View image in fullscreen Brahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought… Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Mohamed Salah, 2026

Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)

Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is that Mo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australia was the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream. RS

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino agrees deal to stay as US coach through World Cup 2030
Sports.content:
US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino and the US Soccer Federation have agreed to a contract extension that will keep Pochettino attached to the program through 2030, US Soccer announced on Monday.

The two sides had been actively engaged in discussions on a contract extension for several months, long before the USMNT’s disappointing, last-16 exit in this summer’s World Cup, with the federation making it clear it desired Pochettino to stay. Conversations picked up in the weeks following the World Cup, with the Guardian reporting last week that the sides had been in the “final stages” of agreeing to a deal. Financial details of the contract extension were not released, but Pochettino is expected to get a raise on top of the $6m per year he earned under his previous deal with the federation – already the largest outlay for a US head coach.

The Guardian understands that billionaire hedge fund manager Ken Griffin, who bankrolled US Soccer’s initial contract with Pochettino, will once again be the primary funder for the new deal. A source familiar with the agreement characterized Pochettino’s return as being in an “expanded role.” Another source said the primary focus of Pochettino and his staff will be on the senior US team, while the federation’s announcement said that the coaching staff will “advise and support” the federation on “the broader development of the full national team pathway, youth soccer, coaching education, professional league collaboration and other technical facets across the soccer community.”

“It has become clear to us that there is tremendous potential to make the men’s national team program even stronger,” Pochettino said in US Soccer’s announcement. “The passion we experienced from the fans throughout the World Cup only strengthened our belief in what is possible here. We are excited by the opportunity to bring all our experience and knowledge to even more areas of U.S. Soccer while helping strengthen the pathways for players, coaches and teams across the Federation.”

Under Pochettino, the US’s World Cup got off to a bright start and featured arguably the program’s best-ever performance at the tournament, a comprehensive, 4-1 dismantling of Paraguay in their group-stage opener. Strong efforts against Australia and Bosnia and Herzegovina followed, setting the stage for the last-16 encounter with Belgium. The US were outclassed in every way in that match, with Pochettino – along with many players – taking the brunt of the blame for the loss.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino’s US team put forth strong performances before crashing out of the World Cup against Belgium. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP

Pochettino is widely liked by players and staff, with some crediting the coach for overhauling the group’s mentality. He clashed with some players who he felt weren’t fully committed, most notably Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic, going as far as to air his grievances publicly. His relationship with the media also came under scrutiny in his tenure, the result of a handful of dust-ups with reporters and journalists who cover the team regularly.

After the USMNT’s crashout against Belgium, Pochettino expressed pride in the work his staff had done with players. He had been at the helm for about 20 months at that point, and Pochettino suggested that the truncated tenure had only been enough to evaluate the group properly and put standards and practices in place.

“With good things and not so good things,” Pochettino told the Guardian after the Belgium loss, “it was amazing, this journey. It still hasn’t been two years working here. And we all know that a process is about a four-year cycle. Today I think we closed the chapter about assessing players, playing in that competition that is so difficult. I think now we have a complete assessment from a lot of players, and if we commit to be here in the future, we have a clear idea of our decisions for the future – before, it was very difficult.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

During his time with the US, Pochettino has put together a respectable record of 18 wins, 12 losses and one draw. His early struggles included a fourth-place finish in the 2025 Nations League and a loss to Mexico in the final of the Gold Cup, a tournament he navigated with a heavily rotated squad. He did have his highlights – the electrifying start to this summer’s World Cup, and a 5-1 thrashing of Uruguay in a friendly that ranks as one of the program’s most surprising results.

Still, Pochettino was largely hired to do one job: advance the US past the last 16 and into the quarter-finals at a home World Cup. He did not manage to do so, but the federation has now offered him another chance to hit that goal in 2030.

Sports.title: Marc Skinner leaves Manchester United Women head coach role amid transfer frustration
Sports.content:
Marc Skinner has left his role as Manchester United’s head coach by mutual consent after five years, partly because of the club’s transfer strategy. The 43-year-old is understood to have initiated the discussions that led to his departure, having felt it was the right time to leave the club. United are focusing on developing young players, rather than enter into bidding wars with some of the Women’s Super League’s bigger spenders.

The former Birmingham and Orlando head coach led Manchester United to three consecutive Women’s FA Cup finals between 2023 and 2025, winning one – and the club’s first major women’s trophy – in 2024 at Wembley with a 4-0 victory over . His side also reached the quarter-finals of the Women’s Champions League in 2025-26, as well as the League Cup final.

Skinner has repeatedly called for greater investment in the team in the transfer market and a change in strategy from the club this summerhas led to his exit.

Skinner oversaw a second-placed finish in the 2022-23 campaign, the club’s highest league position, after a fourth-placed finish in his first season in charge, in 2021-22. United then finished fifth, third and fourth respectively in his final three years in charge.

Sources have indicated the women’s team has a new direction this summer, focused on building a team sustainably with homegrown players, which the club are understood to feel fits their identity of developing youth. Investments are being made into United’s academy.

But other sources have said Skinner was increasingly frustrated at seeing WSL sides outspend United. The sale of French striker Melvine Malard to Chelsea, for a club-record fee in the region of £850,000, has caused concern about the club’s ambition for the upcoming season.

View image in fullscreen Melvine Malard (left) left Manchester United in a club-record sale to Chelsea. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

It comes while London City Lionesses – United’s opponents on the season’s opening day on 4 September – have spent significantly on Spain’s Alexia Putellas and Mapi León, as well as France winger Kadidiatou Diani.

Sources close to the club have indicated they feel such spending is not sustainable in the women’s game. Ultimately, discussions around these matters have concluded with the club and Skinner parting ways before a new campaign when the team can make a fresh start.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Since it became clear Skinner would be leaving, the club have a shortlist of candidates and they are expected to name his replacement relatively quickly.

“Marc leaves having made a significant contribution to the continued progress of Manchester United Women,” United said. “The club places on record its sincere thanks for his professionalism, commitment and dedication throughout his time at United, and wishes him every success in the future.”

Sports.title: Worn in the USA: Liverpool’s pre-season tour had highs but exposed glaring gaps in the squad | Andy Hunter
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour as the Liverpool head coach produced wins over Sunderland in Nashville and Wrexham in New York before ending in a 4-2 defeat against Leeds in Chicago. The Guardian followed the tour throughout and here are a few things we learned.

Iraola’s vision will take time

Liverpool’s second-half display against Leeds was both concerning and valuable for the Iraola as set-piece problems and a tendency to switch off – two of last season’s recurring themes – reared their ugly head again, albeit after he had made changes. Liverpool’s opening 45 minutes, however, was their best of the tour and showed how effective his front-foot, more intense style can be with the big names back. But that process is only just under way.

Iraola is yet to even meet Virgil van Dijk, Cody Gakpo, Alisson, Alexis Mac Allister and new signing Víctor Muñoz since his appointment almost two months ago, never mind coach them. They will be finally be acquainted when the squad reports back for training on Wednesday, having been given a little time off to recover from Sunday night’s flight from Chicago. Mac Allister will be still absent after his World Cup exertions. There is less than three weeks to go and only two more friendlies (although it is a double-header against Como at Anfield) before Liverpool open their Premier League season at Newcastle. “I would like to say on the first day we are going to be perfect, everyone will be in place,” Iraola said. “But probably it is not going to be like this.”

Head coach needs more backing

For most of the tour, Iraola was without eight first-team players due to World-Cup holidays and six because of injury, either recovering from or, as in the unfortunate Joe Gomez’s case, sustained in the US. No prizes for stating that Liverpool’s performances and adaptation to Iraola’s methods would have been much more advanced with 14 extra first-team players available. Even so, glaring gaps remain in the team when every option is taken into account.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool knew about Mohamed Salah’s departure months ago, but have yet to line up a replacement. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

Mohamed Salah’s departure was announced in March. Talks to end his contract one year early commenced earlier. Five months on from the announcement, he is yet to be replaced. The seriousness of Conor Bradley’s knee injury means Liverpool remain light at right-back. There are the highest hopes for Jérémy Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni – the latter has transformed himself into a strapping Adonis while recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury, by the way – while 18-year-olds Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye did well in the US. But Liverpool are lacking Premier League experience in central defence and Ndukwe will be unable to play this season due to post-Brexit work permit difficulties. Gomez’s injury record means he must be considered a bonus when fit, rather than one of four options. It was interesting to hear Iraola explain how he likes wingers to play both flanks, and the advantages of switching them during a game, but Liverpool’s right side could be a problem even if they succeed in signing Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain.

View image in fullscreen Trey Nyoni’s confident and assured displays pressed his case for more Liverpool game time. Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty Images

Nyoni is now firmly in Iraola’s plans

There was an enforced reliance on young players during the tour and Iraola was genuinely impressed by the levels many showed in training and the friendlies. Ndukwe and Talla Ndiaye, as mentioned, Lewis Koumas, Kieran Morrison and Luke Chambers were among them. But no prospect pushed their first team claims further than Trey Nyoni, who grew in stature and confidence with every outing. The 19-year-old and Rio Ngumoha were permanent fixtures in Arne Slot’s squad last season, but while the winger made 19 appearances in the Premier League, including five starts, Nyoni had to settle for six league outings from the bench. On this evidence, there will be many more this season. The midfielder looked immediately at ease with Iraola’s instructions to find forward options as quickly as possible and did so whether under pressure or by creating space for himself with intelligent movement. His pass in the buildup to Florian Wirtz’s goal against Leeds was exquisite and in keeping with his contribution overall. Nyoni said after the Leeds game he knew he had to improve this summer. He was as good as his word.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Jones did not seize chance

To pinch a phrase from Salah, Curtis Jones looked more out than in at times as he enters the final 12 months of his Liverpool contract with increasing interest from the Italian champions, Inter. Unlike Nyoni and Dominik Szoboszlai, the 25-year-old did not adapt comfortably to Iraola’s requirements for a central midfielder and particularly struggled when introduced in the second half against Leeds. But it was his petulant reaction to not receiving the captain’s armband from Szoboszlai against Wrexham that did him fewest favours.

Jones was also overlooked for the captaincy when Gomez exited the opening game against Sunderland. On both occasions the armband was passed to Kostas Tsimikas, a reserve left-back who spent last season on loan at Roma. Of course, that was going to annoy a boyhood Liverpool fan and one of the more senior players on the tour, and Jones, Szoboszlai and Tsimikas all went to great lengths to laugh off the incident in the days after the Wrexham win. The row might have been overblown on social media, but given Iraola stresses the importance of the collective, Jones’s individualistic behaviour jarred with what he is trying to build.

View image in fullscreen Dominik Szoboszlai led the way for Liverpool on the US tour. Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty Images

Szoboszlai wins popularity contest

In the absence of Salah, Andy Robertson, Van Dijk and Alisson, and in keeping with his status as Liverpool’s player of last season, Szoboszlai was undoubtedly the big attraction for fans in the US. The Hungary captain’s every introduction and contribution was met with fanatical acclaim and his was the face the media wanted on their channels. More importantly for Iraola, Szoboszlai led the way in training and his leadership was invaluable given the relative inexperience of the squad. Fresh from signing a new five-year contract, the 25-year-old is an obvious choice to fill one of the vice-captain vacancies created by the departures of Salah and Robertson.

Sports.title: RB Leipzig chief delivers Yan Diomande transfer update amid claims Real Madrid move on hold
Sports.content:
RB Leipzig managing director has emphatically quashed talk that Yan Diomande's switch to Real Madrid was a done deal.

talkSPORT understands the two clubs have a verbal agreement in principle in place for Diomande, with the final details still to be thrashed out.



3 Diomande's days as a RB Leipzig player may be numbered Credit: Getty

But that didn't stop transfer reporter Fabrizio Romano from jumping the gun as he proclaimed on social media the deal had reached the 'here we go' stage, a phrase he uses to indicate when a transfer is complete before it is officially announced.

However, the German club's managing director, Marcel Schafer, has since refuted the claims the deal had been wrapped up.

“It’s clear that some so-called transfer experts reported a few days ago that the deal was done or gave it the ‘here we go,'" Schafer told Sky Germany.



"That’s simply not the case. We’re not at that stage yet.”

How legal troubles could derail Diomande's Real Madrid switch

Further muddying the waters of Diomande's mooted switch to the Bernabeu is a legal dispute between the Ivorian's former representatives and Roc Nation.

Reports in Spain claim Real had been negotiating a deal for Diomande with Roc Nation, a sports agency founded by Jay-Z, having been under the impression they were the player's primary representatives.



But the deal has encountered a hitch as Maxidel Management, an agency led by former Bournemouth winger Max Gradel, has reportedly filed a lawsuit with FIFA, citing a breach of contract.

It is reported Maxidel Management, which oversaw the deal which brought Diomande to Leipzig from Spanish side Leganes last July, maintain they retain the winger's rights until he departs the Bundesliga outfit.



Despite the messy side plot, Schafer does not believe it will result in Diomande's move to Real collapsing entirely.

"From my perspective, it's a clear no," Schafer said.

3 Gradel entered the world of player management after retiring

"I'm not aware of that.

"There has been a change of agents. Our point of contact is now Roc Nation, that's something Yan made very clear to us.

"I don't think a transfer would fall through because of that, if it even comes to a transfer in the first place."



Diomande's future has been a hot topic throughout the summer after a breakout season with Leipzig in which he scored 13 goals in 36 appearances across all competitions to help the club finish third in the Bundesliga.

Liverpool had emerged as a contender early on in the Diomande sweepstakes, only to withdraw from the running once it became clear he favoured a move to Paris Saint-Germain.

Yet the Parisians, who had agreed personal terms with Diomande on a five-year contract, chose not to match Real's offer once they pulled up to the table.

3 Diomande added to his price tag with impressive displays at the World Cup for the Ivory Coast Credit: Getty



Which players have joined Real Madrid this summer?

It has already been a busy summer for Los Blancos, who enter the new season with Jose Mourinho at the helm for a second stint.

Bernardo Silva and Ibrahima Konate both joined the Spanish giants on free transfers from Manchester City and Liverpool respectively.

Real continued to boost their defensive stocks with the acquisitions of Marc Cucurella from Chelsea and Denzel Dumfries from Inter Milan.

But Diomande would undoubtedly be the marquee arrival of the lot as Mourinho looks to restore Real to the top of LaLiga.

Sports.title: Jordan Henderson tipped to emulate Premier League legend at Chelsea as surprise transfer confirmed
Sports.content:
Chelsea have completed the signing of Jordan Henderson on a two-year contract.

The England midfielder has joined the Blues on a free transfer, just days after he had his contract mutually cancelled by Brentford.

4 Henderson joins the sixth club of his career Credit: Getty

Henderson spent a year with the Bees, having joined the club following his exit from Ajax in the 2025 summer transfer window.

The 36-year-old impressed on his shock return to the Premier League, making 32 league appearances last term for Keith Andrews' side.

His performances saw him continue to be selected for England under Thomas Tuchel, and was part of his World Cup squad in North America this summer.

However, Henderson made just one appearance for the Three Lions, with his tournament ending early after surgery on a broken radius, suffering the injury while celebrating England's last 16 win over Mexico.

'I couldn't turn it down'

"Given the size of the club, the manager, who I have great admiration for, and the quality of the players, this was a huge opportunity I couldn’t turn down," Henderson told Chelsea's in-house media.

"I was also so impressed with how much the ownership want Chelsea to be successful and move in the right direction.

"For me, it's about giving everything every single day, both on and off the field, to help the players around me and the team as much as possible. I'm very excited to get going."

Wealth of experience

Now, Henderson adds some much-needed experience to a Chelsea side that struggled for leaders last term.

This is clearly an area the Blues are keen to bolster, with 35-year-old Danny Welbeck also signing, the striker arriving from Brighton over the weekend.

Henderson's year at Brentford came after spells with Ajax and Saudi club Al Ettifaq, which followed his Liverpool exit in 2023.

4 Chelsea's move for Henderson represents a change in the club's transfer strategy this summer Credit: Getty

During his time at Anfield, he won eight major trophies including the Champions League, Premier League and Club World Cup - captaining the Reds to all three successes.

New Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso will be hoping Henderson can instil a winning mentality in his team, whose mentality and maturity came under question at times last term.

The west Londoners had ten dismissals in the 2025/26 season, eight of which came in the Premier League - more than any other side.

Henderson's arrival also follows Chelsea's British-record signing of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117million.

Xabi Alonso's side have also signed defender Marco Palestra from Atalanta already this summer.

4 Xabi Alonso has been tasked with restoring the Blues to their former glories Credit: Getty

'Good senior pros'

Chelsea's decision to sign Henderson has divided opinion, but ex-Blues striker Tony Cascarino hailed it as shrewd business.

Speaking on talkSPORT's Weekend Sports Breakfast, Cascarino insisted both Henderson and Welbeck will help to drive standards and leadership at Stamford Bridge.

He said: “You sign good senior pros. You find out their mentality. There's no doubt in my mind.

“I don't know Danny Welbeck, I'm pretty confident that he is a great lad. And he'll be a great asset to Chelsea.

4 Henderson's leadership qualities were a key reason for his inclusion in England's 2026 World Cup squad Credit: Getty

"He's sorely needed at that football club. Because they've lacked experience on the pitch for a number of seasons now, and I think they've paid a heavy price. And also, say, they lacked experience when Liam Rosenior took the job - they went for a potential young manager.

“I think it's all about the mentality. I always think of Gary McAllister when he went to Liverpool - those type of players. And I think of Teddy Sheringham when he went to Manchester United.

“Yes, they're big clubs. But the mentality of having those senior pros come in, not to run a dressing room, to have a respect in the dressing room for everything that might be wrong.”

On the experience Henderson will provide, Cascarino added: "I think Chelsea have really lost that in their dressing room by ignoring proven players."

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp would have raided Championship club to sign Mohamed Salah replacement
Sports.content:
Jarrod Bowen would already be on the Liverpool books as Mohamed Salah's replacement had Jurgen Klopp still been at the Anfield helm.

That's according to former Premier League midfielder and Liverpool fan Kevin Nolan, who suggested the West Ham captain is the ideal replacement for the Reds icon.

2 Bowen would have replaced Salah already had Klopp stayed on as Liverpool boss Credit: Getty

Salah officially played his final game for Liverpool back in May having confirmed that this season would be his last on Merseyside.

However, despite ample time to prepare for his departure, Liverpool are yet to sign a replacement for the Egypt international.

Yan Diomande was a top target for the 2024/25 Premier League champions, though they have since missed out on the Real Madrid-bound Ivorian.

French winger Bradley Barcola is another on the club's radar, even if the Paris Saint-Germain man operates better from the left rather than Salah's favoured right side.

And as Liverpool scramble to replace the former Roma man, Nolan believes Klopp, who left the Reds in 2024, would have sanctioned the signing of Bowen had the German still been in charge.

Presenter and talkSPORT's chief football correspondent Alex Crook mentioned that while Salah didn't have his best season last season, he still needs replacing, to which Nolan said: "Of course he does.

"I'm surprised Jarrod Bowen wasn't linked. I know when Jurgen Klopp was there, he really really liked Jarrod Bowen and he was high on the priority list.

"I think if Jurgen was still there, I think he probably would be a Liverpool player now."

Take a Bowen, son

Bowen was one of a number of West Ham players linked with a summer exit following the Hammers' relegation last season.

2 Bowen won't be leaving West Ham this summer having penned a new deal at the London Stadium Credit: AFP

The east London side finished two points behind rivals Tottenham Hotspur as they joined Burnley and Wolves in the Championship.

Mateus Fernandes and Crysencio Summerville have both departed the London Stadium for Spurs and Saudi club Al Hilal, respectively, following their relegation.

talkSPORT understands the Hammers are keen on replacing the Dutchman with Spurs winger Manor Solomon.

West Ham skipper Bowen, though, won't be leaving the capital outfit this summer having put pen to paper on a new deal with the Hammers.

However, talkSPORT understands that Bowen is free to leave West Ham next summer should they fail to secure an immediate return to the Premier League.

Nuno's side get their Championship campaign underway with a trip to Turf Moor to face Burnley on Sunday August 16.

Sports.title: Trevoh Chalobah set to leave Chelsea for Champions League club as deal agreed
Sports.content:
Trevoh Chalobah set to leave Chelsea for Champions League club as deal agreed

Como have reached a verbal agreement with Chelsea to sign Trevoh Chalobah, talkSPORT understands.

The deal is worth €30million (£25.7m) as a fixed fee, with €6m (£5.1m) in add-ons.

3 Chalobah is set to join Como in Italy after 19 years at Chelsea Credit: Getty

A sell-on clause has also been agreed for the England international.

Chalobah will return to Champions League football with Como, who make their competition debut in the new season.

The 27-year-old is set to leave Chelsea after nearly two decades at the club having joined their academy in 2007.

Since starting to play regularly for the first team in 2021, he has made 151 appearances across all competitions and scored eight goals.

Chalobah departs after winning two Club World Cups, the FA Cup, the Super Cup and Conference League.

Changes at the back

He is unlikely to be the only centre-back departure from west London this summer.

Axel Disasi and Benoit Badiashile have been linked exits having fallen down the pecking order at Stamford Bridge.

Disasi, who spent the second half of last season on loan at West Ham, is understood to have attracted interest from AC Milan and Roma.

Napoli are reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Chelsea to sign Badiashile.

Levi Colwill looks set to start at centre-back alongside their new £52m signing Maxence Lacroix.

3 Chalobah is one of Chelsea's most successful academy graduates Credit: Getty

Wesley Fofana, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mamadou Sarr are also options for manager Xabi Alonso.

The trio, as well as Colwill, have all played during their pre-season tour in Sydney, with Chelsea now in Hong Kong for the next leg.

Chalobah will be the fourth major summer sale after Marc Cucurella, Tyrique George and Andrey Santos.

In terms of incomings, six other players have joined Lacroix as fresh faces in SW6.

Marco Palestra, Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda were all brought in earlier in the window.

Morgan Rogers then became their record all-time signing in a £117m move from Aston Villa.

The 2026/27 Premier League season is now just days away.

With the World Cup over, the top-flight is ready to return and the countdown is on for the opening game of the campaign.

4 Mikel Arteta's champions face Coventry on the first day of the new season Credit: Getty



And Coventry will get things underway with their first game back in the Premier League for 25 years, facing champions Arsenal.

All 380 games for the 2026/27 season were confirmed in June and also see newly-promoted Hull City hosting Michael Carrick's Manchester United on the opening weekend.

Meanwhile, Tottenham travel to Brentford and feel they have the right manager in charge in Roberto De Zerbi, who guided them to safety on the final day of the 2025/26 season.



And Xabi Alonso's first game as Chelsea boss takes him to Fulham on Monday night, while it could be a changed Man City side that takes on Bournemouth with Elliot Anderson in the middle.

When does the Premier League season begin?

Arsenal, winners last season, begin the new season on Friday, August 21 as they take on Coventry at the Emirates at 8pm.



The top-flight opener will be exclusively live on talkSPORT.

Hull host Man United at 12:30pm on the first Saturday of the season - also on talkSPORT - while Brentford vs Tottenham is the 5:30pm match and there are a trio of 3pm games.

Newcastle vs Liverpool is the first 4:30pm Sunday match of the new campaign.

Hull, who were beaten by Tottenham 7-1 in their last Premier League game in 2017, won't have it easier against a revitalised United side led by Carrick, who was given the manager's role having guided them to third place last season.

Sports.title: Ralf Rangnick’s only Manchester United signing told he can leave permanently this summer
Sports.content:
Ralf Rangnick’s only Manchester United signing told he can leave permanently this summer

Toby Collyer has been reportedly told by Manchester United he is free to pursue a move this summer.

The 22-year-old was not included in the Red Devils squad that ventured to Stockholm for a pre-season friendly against Atletico Madrid last Saturday.



3 Collyer is poised to leave United after four years Credit: Getty

Instead, Collyer turned out for United's Under-21 squad in a 1-0 loss to National League outfit Altrincham Town last Friday.

With his first team future uncertain, The Sun report Collyer received the green light from the club to seek pastures new.

The report adds a number of Championship clubs are interested in signing the 22-year-old, who will become a free agent at the end of the season.



A defensive midfielder by trade, Collyer is unlikely to break into the first team following the summer acquisitions of Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

Tielemans joined the Red Devils from Aston Villa after they triggered his £35million release clause while Santos made the switch from Chelsea for £50m.



Collyer would also have to usurp Kobbie Mainoo, who signed a bumper new deal in April, to crack the starting line-up.

Coll on me

The 22-year-old moved to Old Trafford in March 2023 as an academy prospect from Brighton, making him the only arrival of Ralf Rangnick's interim stint at the club.



He has gone on to make 13 first-team appearances for the Red Devils, but only three were starts.

Collyer's last sighting for United in a competitive fixture came on March 16, 2025, where he enjoyed a 39-minute spell off the bench in a 3-0 win over Leicester City.

The midfielder began the 2025/26 campaign on loan at West Brom but had his deal cut short having sustained a calf injury.

3 Rangnick led United to their lowest Premier League points total during his 29-game interim spell, although the tally has since been beaten Credit: Getty



Prior to his injury, Collyer endured a difficult time at the Hawthorns as he had to wait until his eighth match before he earned a starting berth.

Collyer then joined Hull City on loan for the remainder of the season towards the end of the January window.

However, he featured just five times for the Tigers, who ended the campaign with promotion with a win over Middlesbrough in the Championship play-off final.

Theatre of Screams

Should Collyer secure a move away from United this summer, he would not be the only first team departure.



Jadon Sancho, who joined the Red Devils for an estimated £73m in the summer of 2021, was released upon the expiry of his contract.

The 26-year-old has since been spotted training at 10th tier side Flixton FC while he ponders his next move.

3 Sancho's Old Trafford career produced very few highlights Credit: Getty

Midfielder Casemiro was another who left at the end of his deal, with the Brazilian later joining MLS outfit Inter Miami.



Unfortunately the veteran endured a home debut to forget as he scored an own goal in Miami's 2-2 draw with Columbus Crew.

Sports.title: Major concerns raised over Newcastle’s £140m summer signings
Sports.content:
Kevin Nolan fears Newcastle United's lack of 'Premier League proven' signings could come back to bite them.

The Magpies have already spent over £140million on five new first-team additions this summer.



3 Nolan has expressed fears over Newcastle's summer transfer business Credit: talkSPORT

Goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek became the latest arrival on Monday as he completed a £25.7million move from Braga.

The 24-year-old is the only Newcastle signing during the current window aged older than 21.

Fellow fresh faces Bazoumana Toure, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur and Ewen Jaouen are all 20 or younger.



Meanwhile, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon were both sold earlier in the summer and could be followed out the door by Bruno Guimaraes.

Eddie Howe has also left his role as manager, with Matthias Jaissle set to be named as his successor.



Nolan fears

Nolan has now raised concerns over the club's transfer business, with none of the signings having previous experience of English football.

The former Magpies captain joined Alex Crook live on talkSPORT on Monday morning.



Discussing his old club's incomings, Nolan admitted: "The biggest thing for me is that a lot of these lads who are coming in are not Premier League proven and I think that’s always a problem.

"When you have too many, sometimes it can come back and bite you.

"So I feel like in the next couple of weeks we will hopefully see that they’re going to get some players in who are going to help them young lads to be able to settle into which is the best league in the world.

3 Signings without Premier League experience, such as Steur, concern Nolan Credit: Getty

"You can only do that when you’ve got the experience of doing it, being in it week in, week out.



"I’ve spoken about it on the show before, when these lads come over from the Holland’s, Germany’s, Spain’s and France’s, they find it really difficult because of the intensity and the mentality.

"What’s needed to go and keep going again and that’s one thing which they won’t be used to at all."

Newcastle latest

It has been a summer of change so far at St. James' Park following last season's 12th place finish.

Newcastle missed out on European football by four points as a result, having played in the Champions League during the 2025/26 campaign.



As well as Howe's departure, further players could still leave the club before the end of the transfer window.

Sports.title: When is the Community Shield and why is it not at Wembley? Arsenal face Man City as season opener moved out of England
Sports.content:
When is the Community Shield and why is it not at Wembley? Arsenal face Man City as season opener moved out of England

The Community Shield is a staple of pre-season in England - but it will not be staged in the country for the first time in two decades.

Fans across the world will tune in to watch Premier League champions Arsenal take on FA Cup winners Manchester City.



3 Arsenal could be the team to beat again this season as they look to defend their crown in the Premier League Credit: Getty Images - Getty

The Gunners head into the match aiming to build on their title-winning campaign, following a long-awaited success last term.

Meanwhile, Enzo Maresca will manage his first game as Man City manager and kick off the post-Pep Guardiola era.

Why is the Community Shield not at Wembley Stadium this year?

A major change of venue will see the clash move away from Wembley Stadium to an iconic ground that last hosted the event in 2006.



This is due to scheduling issues with pre-planned summer concerts taking place at the traditional venue.

The Weeknd is booked at England's national football stadium, performing his 'After Hours Til Dawn Stadium Tour with Playboi Carti'.



The official statement released by the FA confirmed supporters will have to cross the border into Wales for the clash.

They stated: "The 2026 FA Community Shield will be played at Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Sunday 16 August."



The event is historically held on the weekend before the Premier League commences, with this season on August 22.

This meant organisers had to target mid-August, which unfortunately clashed with the concert dates.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff, a 74,500-capacity venue, offers a strictly neutral ground for both competing clubs, ensuring that fans of both teams face a journey.

3 Palace won the Community Shield at Wembley last year Credit: Getty



The Welsh national ground has hosted the Community Shield on six occasions between 2001 and 2006.

During that period, Arsenal played in four of the meetings, and won two.

Over the six years the fixture was relocated, only four teams competed across the border: Liverpool, Manchester United, Arsenal, and Chelsea.

In 2022, the fixture was also moved to the King Power Stadium due to Wembley Stadium hosting the Women's Euro 2022 final.



And in 2012, the game was also moved to Villa Park to host Man City and Chelsea as Wembley hosted the final of the 2012 Olympic football tournament.

The Manchester outfit were victorious on the day, winning 3-2.

3 Maresca's first competitive match in charge will be in Cardiff Credit: Getty

When is the Community Shield?

The 2026 FA Community Shield will take place on Sunday, August 16.

Kick-off for the match is scheduled for 3pm and will be held at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.

talkSPORT will have coverage of the fixture, with commentary from Sam Matterface and former England captain Stuart Pearce.

Who won the 2025 Community Shield?

Crystal Palace won last year's edition against Liverpool after securing their first-ever FA Cup.

The Eagles beat the Reds 3-2 on penalties at Wembley after playing out a 2-2 draw in normal time.

Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr scored for Palace in the draw, with Hugo Ekitike and Jeremie Frimpong netting for Liverpool.

Marc Guehi lifted the trophy as captain under Oliver Glasner, but he will be representing Man City on this year's occasion.
