"If someone shows up to a protest and they're prepared to engage in civil disobedience or they spontaneously decide, I'm going to join this line of people who's blocking this detainee transport, I don't think that's enough to show a criminal conspiracy," Terr says.

In a statement, the Justice Department told NPR that federal prosecutors are correct to prioritize these cases.

"People should not mistake violence against law enforcement or impeding officers performing their duties with peaceful protest," the statement said.

Convictions in Spokane

Many of the conspiracy cases against ICE protesters have been dismissed or are ongoing, but the Justice Department is having some success.

Last summer in Spokane, Wash., protesters gathered outside a building where federal immigration officers were holding two immigrants. Some linked arms and tried to block a van from moving the detainees to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. Local police used pepper balls to disperse the crowd and arrested about 30 people.

The day after the protest, the DOJ ordered U.S. attorneys around the country to prioritize prosecuting protesters who destroyed property or assaulted law enforcement, according to an internal email seen by Reuters. A few months later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo directing U.S. attorneys in select districts to charge those protesters, as well as people who interfered with law enforcement, "with the highest provable offense available under the law."

Sponsor Message

After the Spokane protest, Richard Barker, the acting U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Washington, initially asked his prosecutors to look into conspiracy charges for the Spokane protesters, but instead of signing an indictment, he resigned.

About a month after the protest, nine people were charged with conspiracy. Barker's successor had signed the indictment.

Six defendants pleaded guilty, but three chose to go to trial, including Jac Archer and Bajun Mavalwalla II.

toggle caption Margaret Albaugh for NPR

"At the end of the day. I fundamentally couldn't stomach admitting to doing something I know I didn't do," Archer, a longtime organizer, says of the decision to go to trial.

During the trial in May, prosecutors argued that the defendants entered into a conspiracy the day of the protest to block the vehicle transporting detainees.

"Being charged with a federal felony, a conspiracy charge that holds the potential for six years in prison because I showed up to a protest, seems to me to be an attack on a fundamental right that all Americans hold," Mavalwalla, a combat veteran who served in Afghanistan, told NPR.

The government alleged that federal agents feared for their safety that day and that protesters damaged property, including slashing tires. Archer and Mavalwalla were not accused of that in the indictment.

toggle caption Margaret Albaugh for NPR

On the day of the protest, Archer posted a call on social media for others to join, saying some people were choosing to "risk arrest to block the exits to ICE." The federal government cited that post in its indictment. Archer told NPR that any organizer who takes community safety seriously will alert people to that risk before things veer into civil disobedience territory.

All three defendants were found guilty of conspiracy.

"I question whether justice was truly served by today's verdict," Barker, the U.S. attorney who resigned, told The Guardian at the time, describing the case as "a civil war-era law dusted off to punish members of our community who stood up for two young men who were unlawfully detained by ICE."

Sponsor Message

Archer and Mavalwalla's lawyers are exploring next steps, including asking the judge to throw out the verdict, arguing that the evidence was not enough to prove guilt.

"This whole situation is not just beyond my expectations," says Archer, who has attended dozens of protests. "It doesn't align with how I understood things to work."

"An attempt to scare Americans"

Archer and Mavalwalla's story sounds familiar to Joselyn Walsh and Michael Rabbitt. Both were indicted after a protest outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Ill., last September.

On the day in question, video posted on social media shows a federal officer driving toward the group of protesters, and some of them blocking the vehicle.

Prosecutors alleged that some protesters caused damage to it, though Walsh and Rabbitt were not accused of that. They both say they touched the car briefly.

"When you're in a crowd of people that a car drives into, you may end up making contact with that car. But it didn't stick in my mind," says Walsh, a local musician in Chicago.

toggle caption Jamie Kelter Davis for NPR

A month after the incident, Walsh and Rabbitt were charged with conspiracy, along with four others.

"They sought to make an example of us," says Rabbitt, a longtime political activist and the Democratic committeeperson for Chicago's 45th Ward.

This spring, the case against them was dismissed because of alleged prosecutorial misconduct. Even so, Walsh says the experience rattled her.

"I think that what I've learned through this experience is just how much power the federal government really has over our lives and our liberty," she says.

Katie Schwartzmann, legal counsel with the organization Protect Democracy, says more indictments against protesters could be coming.

toggle caption Jamie Kelter Davis for NPR

"It's important to see these indictments and the use of this law for what it is, which is an attempt to scare Americans," Schwartzmann says. "But also, Americans should not be afraid to organize peaceful resistance in this moment. Those acts of ordinary people organizing and working together have been the most important force for justice in the history of our country."

Sponsor Message

NPR's Katie Daugert and Jane Gilvin contributed reporting.

World.title: WestJet, union reach tentative deal to end strike by flight attendants
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet and the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) have reached a tentative deal, ending a strike ​that has led to the cancellation ‌of hundreds of flights, both sides said early Monday.

CUPE, which represents 4,400 flight attendants with the Calgary-based airline, sought pay for its members from ⁠the time they check in until they clock out, instead of ‌mostly just for time when their aircraft is in motion.

The deal ends the work stoppage — which had left passengers stranded and in limbo — during the busy summer travel season after flight attendants walked off the job Sunday.

WATCH | WestJet-CUPE tentative deal's impact on passengers: WestJet, CUPE reach tentative deal, ending strike by flight attendants | Duration 4:43 WestJet and the Canadian Union of Public Employees reached a tentative deal to end a strike by flight attendants after hundreds of flights were cancelled. Pay has been at the centre of the dispute, with the union arguing that unpaid ground duties are not fairly compensated.

WestJet didn't disclose ​details of the tentative agreement, which will be presented to ⁠cabin crew for a ratification ⁠vote.

Minister of Jobs and Families Patty Hajdu confirmed the tentative pact on X, saying "the federal government and Canadians welcome the news that the parties have reached a deal together, at the bargaining table."

Timing for flights to resume

It isn't immediately known when flights will resume fully.

But John Gradek, faculty lecturer in aviation management at McGill University in Montreal, said it will likely take a few days.

"It's about time," Gradek said of the tentative deal, noting that some 225,000 Canadians were affected by WestJet flight cancellations this weekend.

Gradek said the August long weekend — and particularly the holiday Monday — represents the busiest time in the summer for WestJet.

"Today is shot. Things are going to need to get fixed up."

Canadians who've been affected should remain "on guard" and keep checking the latest status of their flights, said Shalene Dudley, a Toronto-based travel agent and CEO of Latitude Concierge Travel.

"It's a scary place to be, especially when you're celebrating something like a wedding."

Travel situation called a 'gong show'

Kevin Stefan has been stranded in Copenhagen with his wife. After not hearing anything for about 24 hours, the couple finally received an email on Monday confirming a new flight, operated by Scandinavian Airlines (SAS), into Boston on Wednesday.

The pair will travel home to Calgary via WestJet, he said.

"So, good news as long as the strike is resolved and SAS actually has our flight unlike last time.," Stefan said.

WestJet communications said the couple were previously rebooked on a different SAS flight, but the Scandinavian carrier couldn't find their tickets.

The two have had to move between hotels as their time in Copenhagen has dragged on.

"We've been told we can bill WestJet for the room and expenses," Stefan said. "We'll see what happens. I'll believe we are being reimbursed the second I see the cash and not one second sooner."

Stefan said he's spoken with other stranded travellers and one descriptor keeps coming up: "gong show."

"It's been pretty exhausting. We have to simultaneously live like we're staying here for days and like we're getting on an airplane in a few hours. We both have a cold, which adds to the miserable factor."

Now, the couple are hopeful they'll finally get to travel back home on Wednesday.

Still, Stefan said that he and his wife don't blame the flight attendants.

"They should be paid for their hours worked."

Some insight into tentative pact

In a statement Monday, the union said that the deal, if ratified, would "improve upon the legacy flight credit system by introducing a duty period premium that recognizes more of the work cabin crew are required to perform," and also increases compensation for that work.

"This tentative agreement represents meaningful progress," CUPE Local 8125 president Alia Hussain said in a statement. "It evolves the flight credit system by recognizing more of the work cabin crew are required to perform and with general increases to compensation for that work.

"To our members, thank you for your solidarity throughout this process. We also want to thank the public, labour organizations and everyone who supported cabin crew as we worked toward a fair resolution."

CUPE is slated to speak with reporters in Calgary at 1 p.m. ET.

CBC News spoke to a passenger who has been visiting St. John's from Toronto and was affected by the strike.

While at the St. John's International Airport, Maddie Young said her direct flight to Toronto was cancelled and WestJet rebooked her on a flight that included five layovers stops, spread out over two days.

"I'd just like to get a more direct flight, so I can get back to work soon."

Young added that she hasn't been able to get through to WestJet by phone, even when she's called in the middle of the night.

For now, Young said, she booked a direct flight with a different airline — but she hasn't been able to cancel her multi-stop, two-day trip back to Toronto with WestJet.

"I'm hoping to get through to someone."

Despite the headache, Young voiced support for WestJet flight attendants.

"I'm happy that the strike is over, and I'm hopeful flight attendants got what they were looking for."

World.title: 'We're all pretty stressed out': Residents in B.C.'s Okanagan flee fast-spreading fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Residents in B.C.'s north Okanagan region say they had to leave their homes, possessions and in some cases their pets behind to escape a rapidly spreading wildfire near Vernon.

CBC News spoke with some of the evacuees at the Westbank Lions Community Centre in West Kelowna, which they said was so busy some people had to sleep in their cars overnight.

Tiffany Wilson, a member of the Okanagan Indian Band, said the Bradley Creek wildfire "just exploded overnight." She said she and her family had already left when they heard that officials were evacuating her whole reserve.

"I was prepared to stay. But yeah, it just got too crazy with the winds today," Wilson said, adding that she left with her daughter and son. "We're all pretty stressed out."

Wilson said the winds were so strong they blew over and crushed her shed. During a media update, officials said winds in the area reached up to 80 km/h.

In the back of her truck, parked in front of the community centre, Wilson had her dog, her rooster and three chickens.

Tiffany Wilson says it's been a stressful day for her and her family. (Brady Strachan/CBC)

According to B.C.'s director of wildfire operations on Sunday, an estimated 5,000 people have been evacuated across the province in the past 24 hours — many of them related to the Bradley Creek wildfire on the northwest side of Okanagan Lake.

The fire was discovered on Friday and as of Sunday afternoon had grown to 26 square kilometres. It's one of six wildfires of note burning in the province.

Many of those evacuated from the Bradley Creek wildfire have headed to West Kelowna to seek refuge, while others have sought shelter in Vernon.

'Mom, we're going'

April Joy says she started to get ready to go with her family when she heard helicopters gathering water from the lake just a couple of blocks from her home.

"And then our power went out and I said, 'Mom, we're going. We're not waiting for the [evacuation order]. We're taking the dog and going,'" Joy said, in front of the same community centre.

April Joy says she had to leave her elderly cats behind when she was told to leave her home because of the Bradley Creek wildfire in B.C.'s north Okanagan. (Brady Strachan/CBC)

Joy said she had to make the difficult decision to leave their elderly cats behind — she didn't think they would withstand the trip in a hot, packed vehicle.

This was the first time Joy had been placed under an evacuation order, but she said signs of the last wildfire in the region were still evident — including in front of her home, where a tree stands half burnt, half alive.

'Stranded in Vernon'

Shantal Copley says she also was worried about a cat left behind in her home.

Copley says she was displaced by the Quilpituk Creek wildfire near Fintry, on the west side of Okanagan Lake.

Copley says she was at work when she found out residents in her neighbourhood might be evacuated. But by the time she left and arrived at her home, police were turning people away.

The Bradley Creek wildfire was first discovered on July 31 and as of Sunday afternoon has spread to 26 square kilometres in size. (Parris McGill)

"It's been quite stressful for me knowing that I wasn't able to go and grab anything from my house and I was basically stranded in Vernon," she told CBC News.

"I couldn't go and see my cat who was stuck at my house and it was just really stressful for me with trying to figure out what to do."

Copley says her parents were able to go back to the house and get the cat and a few essentials, but the family is still stuck in Vernon.

'I don't know if I have a home left'

Speaking to CBC News south of Armstrong, about a kilometre east of the Bradley Creek wildfire, North Okanagan resident Rejane Simpson didn't know what was left of her house.

"I don't know if I have a home left," Simpson said, sobbing. "And if I don't have a home left I don't know where I'm going to go because I sure can't afford the rents that are out there now."

North Okanagan resident Rejane Wilson says she doesn't know what's left of her home. (Jay Bertagnolli/CBC)

Simpson said she was at work when she found out about the fire. She says when she found out the fire was out of control she sped home to get her animals, which she managed to access despite the road there already being blocked by officials.

Luckily, she says, she already had a go bag packed.

"I've tried to look. There's so much smoke I can't tell if my house has been missed or if it's gone," she said, wiping away tears. "It's the not knowing that's so scary."

Simpson says she and her husband built the home together; he passed away two years ago and the thought of leaving all their memories behind was devastating.

World.title: Calgary boy’s death hits home for parents of autistic kids prone to wandering or running away
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At this point, Nada Kader has so many locks, alarms, even duct tape on her doors to prevent her youngest from getting out of their home, she worries about how her family would exit the house if there were to ever be a fire.

Her son, seven-year-old Omar, is non-verbal, and is a “big eloper,” she said.

That means that despite all their efforts, Omar tries to escape on what can be an hourly basis. It means Kader and her husband live in a state of constant hypervigilance, sleeping in shifts on different floors to keep a trained ear on the doors should Omar try to get out in the night.

The recent death of Parker, an 11-year-old non-verbal autistic boy who disappeared from a care facility in Calgary, has brought new attention to the issue of elopement for parents of young children with autism.

For many parents who spoke with CBC News, his story was one that hit far too close to home, reflecting the immense struggles of their day-to-day reality.

And as many parents languish on the waitlist for help, some say it highlights the need for more provincial funding for children like theirs.

‘A constant fear’

Omar is creative when it comes to finding ways to get out, Kader says. When he does, he’ll often do so naked, prompting calls from neighbours, and frequent returns home courtesy of Calgary police.

Recently, Kader woke up in the night to an officer in her bedroom, bringing Omar back.

“There's a constant fear in our house, like when somebody rings the doorbell, we instantly stop and check to see where he is,” Kader said. “He needs one-to-one supervision all the time.”

That sense of fear extends now to her daughter, who Kader says is also diagnosed with autism, and was recently diagnosed with anxiety, having picked up on the tension the family feels.

Nada Kader says her family has become hypervigilant to prevent her seven-year-old son Omar from eloping from their Calgary home. (Submitted by Nada Kader)

There are well-meaning suggestions from other parents: put an AirTag in your child’s shoe, or invest in a GPS tracker like an AngelSense.

But for a child with sensory issues — who escapes without clothes on — those options don’t work.

“At this point, my fear is if something happens to him, you know, the blame can't solely be on us. Because at this point in time, we've exhausted every resource we have,” said Kader.

Why do autistic kids elope?

Elopement occurs when someone wanders away or escapes from a home or caregiver, and is common among autistic children.

An oft-cited statistic comes from a 2012 study in the medical journal Pediatrics, in which nearly half of respondents said their autistic children tried to elope at least once after the age of four.

Missing posters covered the city during the search for Parker. His disappearance and death has sparked calls for an alert for vulnerable children who go missing. (Chelsey Mutter/CBC)

Parker’s case sparked calls for an alert system for missing, vulnerable children, something that Premier Danielle Smith has said the province will look into making available.

In the first police news conference about Parker on July 17, Acting Staff Sgt. Scott Guterson said Parker did not have “an extensive history” of wandering off.

But as Calgary mom Jennifer Norman said, “it just takes a second” for the child to slip away, and a parent’s worst nightmare to begin.

She recently asked her eight-year-old son Oliver, who is autistic and verbal, why he runs away and doesn’t stop, even if he hears her calling out his name.

"He goes ‘well, because I'm too busy,’ like there's too much going on in his mind at the moment,” Norman said.

In some cases, it might be because the child has sensory issues, and goes into “fight or flight” to get away from something bothering them, said Michelle Siegel, founder of Exceptional Abilities, which offers educational services to children of differing abilities.

Justin Lewis, whose 12-year-old son has gotten away before, says it comes down to the fact his child views the world in a different way.

“You see, when a light pole from six different angles is profoundly interesting to you, I suppose sometimes you forget that traffic can be dangerous,” said Lewis. “It's not a lack of intelligence, it's a different type of intelligence.”

Parents describe feeling judged, sense of guilt

Kader said it can be “humiliating” to have her child elope, and face questions from police when he’s returned.

“You feel like a terrible parent,” she said.

At times, Michelle Nelson said she feels “judgy eyes” of other parents, like when she’s holding her six-year-old daughter Allora's arm rather than her hand. She does her best to ignore it — she knows she’s doing all she can to keep her daughter safe — but that can be tough.

And despite her daughter’s proclivity to wander, Nelson said she can’t keep her under lock and key.

“You don't want to just hide her away and say, ‘we can't have these experiences because of how you act,’” she said. “You just have to make sure you put the right things in place to lessen the likelihood of it happening.”

Michelle Nelson with her six-year-old daughter Allora. Despite her daughter's history of elopement, Nelson says it is important they still go out and experience the world. (Submitted by Michelle Nelson)

Other families take a different approach.

“Ultimately, we stopped going places. When [Oliver] was really little, our way of dealing with it was to take us out of harm's way and we became a bit of a recluse,” said Norman.

Siegel’s Exceptional Abilities offers summer day camps for children with autism or disabilities. Elopement is something they keep top of mind.

Doors are locked and watched, and children known to wander off are given one-on-one supervision. Parents text when they’ve arrived for pick-up before the door is opened.

During the day, Siegel it’s a typical camp: kids sing, do crafts, play games.

“A lot of times, our kids don't get to do that and have that full-on experience,” Siegel said.

Waiting for help

CBC News has reported on the estimated 20,000 children stuck on the waitlist for Alberta’s Family Support for Children with Disabilities (FSCD), with some families waiting years.

Parents approved through the program are assigned a caseworker and receive funding that might be allocated towards things like respite services in or out of the home, or specialized counselling.

The 2026 provincial budget provided $271 million for FSCD. In June, press secretary to the Minister of Assisted Living and Social Services Amber Edgerton said the ministry is “reviewing the program to ensure effective support for families in need, now and into the future.”

A makeshift memorial for Parker, near the spot where his body was located after his nearly two-week disappearance. (Chelsey Mutter/CBC)

Norman praises the help her son's received through FSCD, saying it has helped improve his habit of eloping.

But she said the problem is how long it takes to get that help. It took her family about 15 months from the time they were approved to get a caseworker, and she says early intervention is key for children with autism.

And for parents like Omar’s mom Kader, who is still waiting for help, it takes a toll.

“You’re mentally exhausted with the wait and the bureaucracy,” Kader said. “It’s frustrating on that level, but at the same time you're doing it with nothing left in the tank. You're exhausted.”

World.title: Meet Saskatchewan's threatened 'butcher bird' that impales its prey
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The songbirds appear to be soft-feathered and pudgy. When they fly, the white patches on their grey and black wings flash in the sun.

But come feeding time, these birds turn into ruthless killers. They catch prey such as bugs, mice and frogs, and impale them on thorns or barbed wire before feasting.

These are loggerhead shrikes — a threatened species colloquially known as a "butcher bird." Their main breeding ground on the Prairies is in Saskatchewan, but wildlife advocates say their habitats are slowly disappearing.

Saskatoon birder Kerry Hjertaas, 42, saw shrikes in action in a field beside his office this summer.

One day, as Hjertaas was getting into his car, a shrike flew onto the barbed-wire fence beside the parking lot and impaled some prey on the wire, he said. A second shrike flew over to also feast on the prey.

"They each started ripping chunks out of it and it disappeared pretty fast," he said. "I was just like, well, I've read about this, but this was super cool to see it in person."

WATCH | Meet Saskatchewan's threatened 'butcher bird' that impales its prey: Meet Saskatchewan's threatened 'butcher bird' that impales its prey | Duration 1:54 The loggerhead shrikes are a threatened species colloquially known as a "butcher bird." Their main breeding ground on the Prairies is in Saskatchewan, but wildlife advocates say their habitats are slowly disappearing.

Shrikes kill that way because they are songbirds, so their dainty feet don't have talons, said Emily Putz, the habitat stewardship co-ordinator of Nature Saskatchewan's shrubs for shrikes program.

Shrikes are the only birds in Saskatchewan that kill like that, she said.

"They're such a unique bird with such unique behaviours," Putz said. "It's really cool to see them in action."

Emily Putz says the 'butcher bird' is unique in Saskatchewan. (Kirk Fraser/CBC)

A threatened species

An estimated 40,000 shrikes are left in Saskatchewan, Putz said. They are a threatened species, which is considered one step below endangered.

Habitat loss is hitting shrikes hard, Putz said.

The birds rely on native prairie to nest and hunt, she said, but Saskatchewan only has about 13 per cent of its native prairie left. So, Putz said, they've adapted to make their homes in shelterbelts, which are shrubs planted around the perimeter of fields.

Loggerhead shrikes can kill their prey by impaling it on barbed wire. (Submitted by Kerry Hjertaas)

But that, too, is under threat as some landowners and farmers take out shelterbelts to use larger machinery on their fields, Putz said.

"So [shrikes are] kind of being hit with a double whammy of losing their native and adapted habitat," she said.

Even the shrikes near Hjertaas's office may have to relocate in the coming years. Their current field, east of Hampton Village and Westview, is slated for commercial development, he said.

Hjertaas said it will be "a little bit sad" to not have shrikes in the area, but added they will likely head out to other fields, where he can still catch a glimpse.

In a statement, the City of Saskatoon said while shrikes are seen around the city, it is "not aware of any designated critical habitat for loggerhead shrike near Saskatoon."

Developers should scan the area for bird nests before construction, the city said. If a shrike nest is found, "appropriate buffers would be established around the nest to protect it."

Shrikes are losing both their native and adapted habitats, Emily Putz says. (Submitted by Kerry Hjertaas)

Protecting shrikes

Every year, Nature Saskatchewan records reported shrike sightings and surveys fields for local shrike populations, Putz said.

As someone who enjoys observing wildlife, Hjertaas said he reported his sightings to the organization to help protect the birds.

"Having them protected means that they're still around," he said. "They're filling their niche in the ecosystem."

A.E. Wilson Park in Regina is home to a loggerhead shrike nesting area. (Kirk Fraser/CBC)

Putz said the public can also help by planting thorny shrubs for shrikes to use, including buffalo berry and hawthorn shrubs.

"It's a unique species. It's great pest control," Putz said. "It's important that we do everything we can to help them along so that the next generation can see them."

World.title: Are there climate benefits to Canada's new relationship with China?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Canada announced earlier this year that it would allow a token number of Chinese-made electric vehicles into the country, the gesture didn't seem so much about climate action as a sop to ease Chinese tariffs on Canadian canola.

Now, it very much appears like the opening gambit in a deeper engagement with China on clean energy. Following up on Prime Minister Mark Carney's momentous meeting with Chinese Premier Xi Jinping in January , Industry Minister Melanie Joly was in Beijing last month to discuss the feasibility of Canadian-Chinese EV ventures.

Meanwhile, the Canada China Business Council is organizing a cleantech mission to China in Beijing in November.

While Carney has gone to great lengths recently to placate Canada's fossil fuel industry — most notably by promising a new pipeline to the B.C. coast — some experts suggest a new relationship with China could provide an efficient way to get back on track with the clean energy transition that much of the rest of the world is already undertaking.

An aerial view of the solar panels at the CNNC Tianwan tidal flat photovoltaic power plant in Lianyungang, in China's eastern Jiangsu province, on April 19. (CN-STR/AFP via Getty Images)

"China is a global clean energy superpower," said Rachel Doran, executive director of Clean Energy Canada, and given the size and sophistication of China's sector, Canada "can't have a strategy around the transition that the world is experiencing without having a strategy around China."

"I think that has motivated some of what the [Canadian] government has tried to do."

China as clean-energy partner

China's dominance in clean-energy manufacturing is staggering . It's responsible for around 80 per cent of the world's solar panels, 60 per cent of wind turbines and 75 per cent of electric vehicles and their batteries, according to the Climate Action Tracker.

Earlier this year, Chinese manufacturer BYD surpassed Tesla in global EV sales for the first time. To illustrate its rapid rise, China went from exporting 28,000 EVs in June 2019 to exporting 316,000 in June 2026.

A woman takes a selfie in front of electric vehicles by Chinese EV manufacturer XPeng in the Port of Guangzhou, China's southern Guangdong province, in February 2025. (Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images)

China is already partnering with other countries on clean energy — such as a venture with the United Arab Emirates to build out wind and solar projects in the Global South .

Accordin g to Bijan Ahmadi, executive director and COO of the Canada China Business Council, there are opportunities for Canada to align "with China’s manufacturing scale, capital and ability to deploy technology rapidly."

"The new Canada-China strategic partnership provides a foundation for this work, specifically identifying clean technology, batteries, solar, wind and energy storage as areas for potential cooperation, " he said.

Back in 2024, Canada imposed 100 per cent tariffs on Chinese EVs, largely at the behest of our southern neighbours. Moe Kabbara, CEO of Canadian non-profit Transition Accelerator, thinks Carney's decision to allow a small number of Chinese EVs into the country was a smart overture.

"It recognizes that Chinese electric vehicles are going to be unavoidable for the North American market," he said. "That should be applauded, in terms of departing from the U.S. on a very important trade policy issue."

WATCH | Trump says he doesn't need Canada as Carney heads to China: Trump says he doesn’t need Canada as Carney heads to China | Duration 2:00 As Prime Minister Mark Carney heads to China to ease trade tensions, President Donald Trump reiterated that the U.S. doesn’t need Canadian goods or the CUSMA. Carney was also urged by Ontario’s premier to not back down on tariffs for Chinese EVs.

Kabbara says it also telegraphed a strategy: Rather than letting Chinese EVs overwhelm the domestic market, the Canadian government is trying to find ways to make it mutually beneficial.

During her recent trip to Beijing, Joly met with five Chinese EV companies in order to negotiate a way to trade selective exposure to the Canadian market for information-sharing and potential joint ventures that, as Kabbara put it, would "allow us to have an auto sector that continues to be vibrant and prosperous."

He said it's a bit of a role reversal.

"The Chinese used the model of joint ventures and tech transfers and IP transfers in the '80s and the '90s to build up their auto sector with Western automakers. Now, the script has flipped, where we have an opportunity to actually learn from the Chinese when it comes to electric vehicles, battery technology and supply chain optimization."

Critical access to minerals

Canada's oil and gas is obviously of interest to a country with a population as large as China's, but Kabbara said that's a short-term advantage.

In the longer term, he said, one thing that makes Canada an attractive partner to China is our critical minerals — such as copper, cobalt and chromium — which would allow us to establish domestic supply chains for clean-energy manufacturing of solar panels, wind turbines and batteries.

Industry players say the attitude between the two countries has changed. Wenran Jiang, president of the Canada-China Energy and Environment Forum, wrote last month in the Edmonton Journal that "after years of frosty diplomacy and mutual suspicion, Canada and China are quietly getting back to business in the energy sector, and they are doing it with a refreshing sense of pragmatism."

WATCH | China looking for trading partners that 'don't use energy for coercion,' Hodgson says: China is looking for trading partners that 'don't use energy for coercion,' Hodgson says | Duration 1:22 Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, who took questions alongside Industry Minister Mélanie Joly during a trip to China, did not offer specific details when asked about potential energy exports to China but said officials there are looking for reliable partners and 'want more of what we've got.'

For one thing, China offers Canadian cleantech businesses a market that's already much further along in the energy transition. In May, China's Envision Energy and Canada's Cape Breton China Corp. announced a strategic partnership with plans to develop a hybrid wind and battery storage project in Sydney, N.S.

Ahmadi from the Canada China Business Council says the cleantech mission to Beijing this fall was developed "in response to growing interest from Canadian clean-technology companies seeking opportunities in China’s low-carbon economy."

The aim of the mission is "to help Canadian companies assess the market, meet potential customers, investors and partners, build commercial relationships and diversify their export opportunities."

Addressing security, privacy risks

While China is leading the way on this transition, relying on the country too heavily for Canada's clean energy solutions is not without its challenges — or critics.

The EV imports, minimal as they may be, have spooked many auto industry insiders over fears that cheap Chinese EVs would undercut the domestic market already threatened by Trump's ongoing tariff strategy.

Detractors also raise worries about security and privacy issues in integrating Chinese-made technology. Kabbara says one possible advantage of better relations with China is that "we can have Canadian software on Chinese hardware that mitigates security concerns."

Doran from Clean Energy Canada says doing more business with China — which remains a one-party state — is an acknowledgement that geopolitical calculations have changed.

"There are signals that Canada is trying to think of China in new ways," said Doran. "We know we want to move towards electrification, and we need to think about doing that cost-effectively and in a smart way as a smaller country, so that we can benefit from the world as it is, and not the world as we want it to be."

World.title: Jays trade 3 prospects to land Los Angeles Angels pitcher Jose Soriano
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Toronto Blue Jays have acquired right-handed pitcher Jose Soriano from the Los Angeles Angeles in exchange for infielder Arjun Nimmala, outfielder Eddie Micheletti Jr., and right-handed pitcher Angel Rivero.

The 27-year-old Soriano from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, has a 9-6 record and a 3.29 earned-run average over 22 starts this season for the Angels.

He was the American League's pitcher of the month for March-April after going 5-1 with a .84 ERA and 49 strikeouts. Soriano's career record is 26-27 with a 3.72 ERA over four seasons.

Nimmala, 20, has split his season between four levels of minor league ball in Toronto's system. The shortstop was selected 20th overall in the 2023 draft.

Michelleti Jr., hit 20 doubles, four triples and 14 home runs for 45 RBI with double-A New Hampshire this season. The left-handed hitter was chosen by the Blue Jays in the eighth round of the 2024 draft.

Rivero, 19, carried a 2.46 ERA over 12 appearances in rookie ball with 52 strikeouts this season. The Venezuelan was signed as an international free agent in 2024.

World.title: As a paramedic, I responded to countless overdoses. Then my best friend died from one
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is written by Cam Fenton, who lives in Cultus Lake, B.C. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

It was mid-morning and the rain was coming down in sheets as we drove the ambulance. My partner and I had been paged out for a “man down” in a parking lot. He was unresponsive and barely breathing, the water soaking his clothes and bouncing droplets off his forehead. Our bag-valve mask made an audible pop as it opened. I connected it to the oxygen tank and my partner squeezed, taking over the patient’s failing breaths while I drew some Naloxone into a syringe.

“Point-four milligrams going into the left lateral thigh,” I said.“ Copy zero-point-four,” my partner replied as I injected the medication. “No change,” my partner noted.

“Drawing up another zero-point-four,” I responded. “Right thigh.”

The patient’s eyes snapped open a few seconds later. When he tried to take a deep breath, he started choking.

“Try to cough. You have a piece of plastic in your throat,” my partner said. The patient spat out the plastic airway I had used to keep his tongue from choking him.

"I hate Narcan," he muttered.

Naloxone is administered by nasal spray or injection and is used to treat overdoses of opioids such as fentanyl, heroin and morphine. (Aura Carreño Rosas/CBC)

A couple of years earlier, I might have ignored the comment. But this time, something gnawed at the back of my head.

"Believe me," I said. "It's better than the alternative."

The moment that shattered me

In the spring of 2023, I got a phone call that changed my life. One of my closest friends had been found unresponsive in his apartment. Paramedics would have called him Code 4, shorthand for a patient that’s beyond any hope of resuscitation. Ben had overdosed.

Naloxone, the same drug I used to reverse overdoses as a paramedic, might have saved his life. It felt like cruel irony when I learned he had been found with the medication beside him. Had he not been alone, someone might have been able to resuscitate him.

Ben’s death hit me like a freight train. Part of it was shock and grief, but another part was anger.

I had lost count of the number of overdose calls I had responded to as a paramedic. They blurred together, from city street corners to rural basements. Some patients recovered quickly. Others took longer. Some didn’t respond to Naloxone at all, thanks to synthetic opioids and drugs like benzodiazepines and xylazine — also known as tranq — being mixed into the drug supply.

Ben knew all this. He worked for a supportive housing organization in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside and occasionally oversaw supervised consumption sites. I even remember one time when he texted me after resuscitating a woman who had overdosed outside his work.

The more I thought about this, the angrier I got. Sometimes, I quietly resented that my patients survived. “Why did they get to live when Ben didn’t,” I would silently wonder.

Fenton, left, with his best friend, Ben Sir, in 2001 on a trip to Blue Springs State Park in Florida. (Submitted by Cam Fenton)

I was being overtaken by compassion fatigue, an all too common reality for first responders and health-care workers that the Canadian Medical Association describes as the “cost of caring for others or for their emotional pain.” It’s also something that is bleeding into how our society views the opioid crisis.

It’s been a decade since British Columbia declared overdoses to be a public health emergency . But despite policies supporting widespread Naloxone and supervised consumption sites saving thousands of lives (a University of British Columbia study estimated overdose death numbers would be 2.5 times higher were it not for harm reduction programs), the crisis persists.

In fact, when Ben died in 2023, he was one of 2,511 people in B.C. who died from toxic drugs that year , a record high for the province. This persistent crisis has fostered compassion fatigue on a massive scale. Public opinion has turned away from harm reduction and towards prohibition, with politics following suit. B.C. is moving ahead with involuntary care , expanding a policy used to institutionalize people experiencing mental health emergencies to allow drug users to be placed, against their will, into treatment beds.

April 14, 2026, marked 10 years since officials in British Columbia declared the toxic drug crisis a public health emergency. Fenton's friend, Ben, is one of those people who died from an overdose. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

In some ways, I get it. For a long time, every overdose I managed reminded me of Ben. But over time, some light has cracked through. I realized that, like Ben, all of my patients have friends and families. That, somewhere out there, they mean as much to someone as Ben did to me.

One more chance

I helped my patient from the wet concrete onto the stretcher, then cranked the ambulance's heat and handed him an extra blanket. He told me he was using "down," a street term for fentanyl. It was, he said, his first time using after a long stint in treatment. I made a note to tell the nurses, just in case he might be willing to go back.

A part of my brain still held onto that compassion fatigue, reminding me that I was more likely to see this patient in the back of another ambulance than on the road to recovery. But then I remembered Ben and thought about what I wouldn’t give to have one more chance, no matter how small, to help him.

I handed the man a small white ondansetron tablet. “Let it dissolve under your tongue. It’ll help with the nausea,” I said. I unwrapped a small plastic vomit bag and laid it on his lap.

“Just in case,” I added.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: After 8 years and 15,000 kilometres, B.C. couple nears end of Trans Canada Trail trek
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Vancouver Island couple is just steps away from completing a journey of over 15,000-kilometre on foot.

Langford's Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain have been walking the length of the Trans Canada Trail in stages, a trek they began in 2018 in St. John's, Newfoundland.

On Saturday, they'll finish the final stretch to Mile Zero in Victoria.

CBC Victoria's Alex Wauthy caught up with them near Mount Wells to get an inside look at an epic journey.

LISTEN | Langford couple steps away from completing trans-Canada walk: On The Island 9:26 South Island couple nearly finished goal of walking across Canada CBC Victoria's Alex Wauthy caught up with Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain, a South Vancouver Island couple who trekked across Canada by foot.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

What made you want to do this?

Julie: We've done a lot of long-distance hiking ... and at the 150th anniversary of Canada, the Trans Canada Trail opened. So we decided, hey, that sounds like a good plan.

Simon: It sounded like a challenge for us. We knew we weren't going to walk all season. At first we thought it was going to be four summers. It turned into eight because of COVID.

The couple cross the Kinsol Trestle near Shawnigan Lake on Vancouver Island during the final stage of their more than 15,000-kilometre journey along the Trans Canada Trail. (Submitted by Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain)

What has this journey been like?

Julie: Long journeys like that, you can never think about the end because it's usually too far away. So you think of it in small bites.

It hasn't sunk in yet that we've actually walked over 15,000 kilometres.

What are some of your highlights?

Julie: For me it's the people.

Strangers giving us ice water when we were walking on roads when it was really hot. Strangers inviting us into their homes for showers or sleepovers or home-cooked meals. Friends joining us for certain sections.

Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain take in the fall colours along the Voyageur Trail near Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., during their cross-Canada journey in 2019. (Submitted by Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain)

Simon: Waking up in Gray Creek Pass in the Kootenays.

Snow all over the place in early June and I could hear some noise around me. I unzipped the tent, looked out and there's a herd of elk just a few metres away and you just sit there and you're in awe.

How would you assess the trail?

Julie: It's a new trail, so there's still some hiccups.

It's not for long-distance walkers because we can be told, 'Oh, there's a campground 40 kilometres away that you can sleep at.' Well, 40 kilometres is two days of walking.

The trail sometimes is closed, but the application won't tell us because it's not updated.

Simon: It's made up of trails from somewhere short of 400 different municipalities ... and some have done an incredible job.

Lanoix and Chatelain during their hike through Alberta’s Badlands in 2023. (Submitted by Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain)

Newfoundland, unbelievable. The T'Railway is one of a kind.

Prince Edward Island and Quebec have incredible infrastructure for cycling and walking.

And then there are some provinces who just don't have the infrastructure or the trail system, so they're connected by roads. So we do a lot road walking.

What have you learned about each other?

Julie: We are a good team. We don't always focus exactly on the same thing and I think that's a really good thing. I'm a micromanager, so I look at the details of food and equipment and things like that. And Simon loves to map out our routes.

The couple can be seen making their way along a snow-covered section of Le P’tit Témis in Quebec in 2019, hauling their gear. (Submitted by Simon Lanoix and Julie Chatelain)

Simon: We took this on 30 years into our marriage... For newlyweds, that might be a challenge.

Sometimes during the day, we're just in our heads. I used to ask Julie, 'What are you thinking of?' She never used to say [this] before, but now, regularly it's 'Nothing' because there's an empty box there, which is beautiful, right?

Lanoix and Chatelain shelter inside their tent during their hike in Sudbury, Ont., in 2019 (Simon Lanoix)

What will it feel like when you reach mile zero?

Julie: I'm already crying about it. I've been fantasizing about having some of our good friends that live locally join us and pretty much everybody has said that they would ... so being surrounded by really good people that we love it's a gift.

Simon: It just feels like I know Canada so much more having done it in slow motion, and by that I mean walking. You just get to appreciate every moment along the way.

World.title: Snow Forecast for Seven Chilean Regions, Including Santiago
World.content:
Heavy rain, strong winds, and snowfall expected as new frontal system approaches

SANTIAGO â Chile’s central and southern regions are preparing for a powerful frontal system bringing wind, rain, and snow over the coming days, according to updated forecasts from the DirecciÃ³n MeteorolÃ³gica de Chile (DMC). The system is expected to benefit water reserves, with substantial snowfall anticipated across the Andes from the Coquimbo to BiobÃ­o regions.

Alerts issued for high winds and snowfall

The DMC has issued weather alerts for much of central Chile due to moderate to strong winds and heavy precipitation. Gusts may exceed 80 km/h in areas from ValparaÃ­so to Ãuble, driven by a low-level jet stream. The strong winds may cause fallen branches, power outages, and “whiteout” conditions in mountainous regions.

Whiteout conditions occur when fresh, uncompacted snow is lifted and dispersed by strong winds, significantly reducing visibility.

Significant rainfall totals expected

ValparaÃ­so Region : Up to 30 mm of rain, mainly overnight Wednesday into Thursday morning.

: Up to 30 mm of rain, mainly overnight Wednesday into Thursday morning. Santiago Metropolitan Region : Similar rainfall amounts concentrated on Thursday morning.

: Similar rainfall amounts concentrated on Thursday morning. OâHiggins Region : Heavier rainfall with up to 40 mm expected on Thursday.

: Heavier rainfall with up to 40 mm expected on Thursday. Maule, Ãuble, and BiobÃ­o Regions: Extended rainfall through Tuesday, June 17, with accumulations likely exceeding 100 mm during the holiday weekend.

Additionally, the DMC has warned of possible thunderstorms on Thursday in Maule, Ãuble, and BiobÃ­o due to post-frontal atmospheric instability, which may generate convective clouds with lightning.

Possible snowfall and sleet for Santiagoâs eastern sectors

The frontal system is accompanied by colder temperatures, increasing the likelihood of snow not only in the high mountains but also in lower pre-Andean areas closer to populated zones.

High likelihood of snow in San JosÃ© de Maipo, San FabiÃ¡n de Alico, Las Trancas, and Farellones.

in San JosÃ© de Maipo, San FabiÃ¡n de Alico, Las Trancas, and Farellones. Potential sleet (aguanieve) in eastern Santiago neighborhoods such as Lo Barnechea, upper La Reina, and PeÃ±alolÃ©n between Thursday evening and early Friday.

These wintry conditions are welcomed by both residents and the tourism industry, as ski centers and mountain resorts benefit from fresh snowfall.

Cold snap to follow weekend storm

Once precipitation subsides, temperatures are expected to drop sharply starting Friday:

Santiago Metropolitan Region : Lows near 2Â°C, highs not exceeding 14Â°C.

: Lows near 2Â°C, highs not exceeding 14Â°C. ValparaÃ­so Coast : Minimums around 6Â°C, dropping to 1Â°C inland.

: Minimums around 6Â°C, dropping to 1Â°C inland. OâHiggins, Maule, Ãuble Regions : Minimums near 2Â°C, highs below 13Â°C.

: Minimums near 2Â°C, highs below 13Â°C. Talca and CuricÃ³: Expected to record lows of 0Â°C on Saturday morning.

The cold spell could persist for several days, prompting authorities to advise residents to prepare appropriate clothing, ensure home heating, and prioritize care for vulnerable groups, including the elderly and young children.

Another frontal system possible Sunday

Meteorologists are closely monitoring the development of a second system forecast to impact central Chile on Sunday, June 15. Early estimates suggest additional rainfall of up to 40 mm for ValparaÃ­so and the Santiago Metropolitan Region, which may exacerbate soil saturation and pose travel disruptions if storms continue in quick succession.

The active weather pattern aligns with the seasonal transition into winter, marked by increased precipitation, colder temperatures, and more frequent snowfall across the Andes.

World.title: Universidad de Chile Eliminated by Curicó Unido in Copa Chile Upset
World.content:
CuricÃ³ Unido advances to quarterfinals after dramatic second-leg draw

SANTIAGO â Defending champions Universidad de Chile have been eliminated from the Copa Chile Coca Cola Sin AzÃºcar 2025 after a 2-2 draw against CuricÃ³ Unido on Wednesday night at Estadio Nacional. The aggregate score favored the visitors, who secured a surprising quarterfinal berth.

Early hopes fade for Universidad de Chile

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
