World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Milei says he has chosen a 2027 running mate amid rupture with his vice president
World.content:
Milei says he has chosen a 2027 running mate amid rupture with his vice president

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 07:24 UTC Full article

He said he has settled on his running mate for next year but prefers to keep the name to himself for now, in an interview published on Sunday by Diario Río Negro

Argentine President Javier Milei said he has already decided who will run alongside him as vice-presidential candidate in the October 2027 elections, while withholding the name, in remarks that come amid an open confrontation with his current vice president, Victoria Villarruel.

He said he has settled on his running mate for next year but prefers to keep the name to himself for now, in an interview published on Sunday by Diario Río Negro. The wording implies he will not repeat the 2023 ticket. Milei and Villarruel are not on speaking terms and criticize each other publicly; Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli called for her resignation after remarks she made about the president. Argentina's constitution permits one consecutive re-election.

Milei had already confirmed weeks earlier, at an event at the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, that he would seek a second term. The new element is the choice of a vice-presidential candidate.

In the same interview he renewed his call to abolish the open, simultaneous and mandatory primaries, putting their cost to the state at 250 million dollars a year, and argued parties should settle internal contests without public funding. The primaries were suspended for the 2025 elections and their status for 2027 has not been settled.

The president also confirmed that the overhaul of the central bank's charter will be the government's main legislative initiative this semester. The bill, submitted to the Chamber of Deputies on Friday, establishes preserving the value of the currency as the institution's sole mission and bars all channels of financing to the Treasury. Central bank presidents need to be shielded from removal by whoever holds power, he said.

On the economy, Milei said results are exceeding expectations and credited his administration with maintaining a fiscal surplus, slowing inflation, lifting currency controls and rebuilding reserves. He projected the country will post three consecutive years of growth for the first time in fifteen years and said economic activity had surpassed its historical peak. These are the president's own assertions, without independent verification.

He acknowledged that part of the population has yet to feel the improvement, saying it is normal that some Argentines do not yet see the trend in their pockets, that fixing in two years what took a century to break requires time, and that he will not offer shortcuts.

Milei also highlighted the incentive regime for large investments, citing more than 46 billion dollars in approved projects and over 100 billion under evaluation, with particular weight in the Patagonian provinces. At the Stock Exchange he had pledged that, if growth holds, his government would by 2031 have returned 500 billion dollars to Argentines through tax cuts.

World.title: Conflicting accounts over whether Spanish intelligence warned of mass entry into Ceuta
World.content:
Conflicting accounts over whether Spanish intelligence warned of mass entry into Ceuta

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 07:20 UTC Full article

The newspaper The Objective reported that intelligence assessments had flagged a possible mass entry into Ceuta and Melilla coinciding with Morocco's Throne Day

Spanish intelligence services concluded that Morocco did not plan last Thursday's mass entry of people into Ceuta, although it allowed the crossings and drew political benefit from the international attention, according to sources cited by El País. Other reporting contradicts that account on a key point: whether the government was warned in advance.

The newspaper The Objective reported that intelligence assessments had flagged a possible mass entry into Ceuta and Melilla coinciding with Morocco's Throne Day. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said in Ceuta on Saturday, by contrast, that the intelligence services gave no warning of what was building on the other side of the border. Both versions rest on unidentified sources, and the Defense Ministry has neither confirmed nor denied them, citing the classified status of National Intelligence Center reports.

Morocco commented publicly for the first time on Monday, attributing the events to human trafficking networks, disinformation and misreadings of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling. Spain's Interior Ministry and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hold the same view of the trigger.

That ruling, issued by the administrative chamber, established that people reaching Ceuta and Melilla by swimming cannot be summarily returned without a formal procedure. It does not declare border returns illegal nor amend immigration law: it sets binding interpretation of an existing provision. A distorted reading circulated on social media and messaging groups spread the notion that Spain would not repatriate those who entered.

Maritime arrivals had been rising through July, with Civil Guard unions warning of inadequate resources. On Thursday, coinciding with the Moroccan holiday, border surveillance was scaled back and then withdrawn. The provisional toll on Monday stood at at least 72 dead, most of them drowned. A comparable episode occurred in 2021, involving between 8,000 and 10,000 people, amid a diplomatic crisis over Spain's hosting of the Polisario Front leader.

Sánchez sent a letter to European institutions criticizing the response of some member states, describing as selfish, polarizing and unlawful measures such as Italy's reintroduction of border checks and proposals from Finland and Denmark to exclude Spain from the Schengen area. A group of 22 countries favoring tighter migration controls requested a meeting of EU interior ministers, scheduled for Tuesday.

On Friday, Sánchez described the events as an attack and a violation of Spain's territorial integrity, though the government has not named Morocco as responsible and has not convened the National Security Council. The Defense Ministry placed some 1,600 troops at the Interior Ministry's disposal for surveillance duties. Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish territory; Morocco maintains a claim over both cities.

World.title: A child's death in Argentina reopens debate over court-ordered family reunification
World.content:
A child's death in Argentina reopens debate over court-ordered family reunification

2nd Sunday, August 2026 - 21:39 UTC Full article

The case drew national attention because of what preceded it. Two other daughters of Sosa died in similar circumstances: one aged six months in 2013 and another aged eleven months in 2016

The death of a two-year-old girl in Villa Gesell, on the coast of Buenos Aires province, and the detention of her mother have drawn scrutiny to Argentina's child protection system, and in particular to court-ordered family reunification proceedings.

The girl was admitted without vital signs on July 21 at the Arturo Illia municipal hospital. An autopsy found she died of hypoxemia caused by obstructive asphyxia. Her mother, Lucía Sosa, 43, said the child had choked. She was detained on July 27 and charged with abandonment resulting in death, aggravated by the family relationship. She declined to testify on her lawyer's advice, and prosecutor Juan Pablo Calderón is weighing whether to reclassify the charge. The detention does not constitute a conviction, and her criminal responsibility must be established through the proceedings. Sosa's partner has also been charged; their four-year-old son has been placed under judicial custody.

The case drew national attention because of what preceded it. Two other daughters of Sosa died in similar circumstances: one aged six months in 2013 and another aged eleven months in 2016. Over the second case, she and her then-partner, Héctor Javier Picart, spent close to two years in detention and were acquitted in 2018 by Criminal Court No. 3 in Mar del Plata. The court reviewed the medical reports, ruled out traumatic injuries and signs of sexual abuse in both girls, attributed the deaths to respiratory complications and concluded that child abuse had not been established.

Two of Sosa's older children, one of them a minor, gave statements to prosecutors this week. Both were hospitalized as infants with asphyxia and later adopted by other families. They say they reported violence for years without being heard, and describe the reunification period — the years in which the courts maintained contact with the biological household before granting permanent custody — as an experience of mistreatment. The elder daughter added an allegation of sexual abuse to the case. None of these accusations has been established in court.

Their lawyer, Erika Hooft, who has followed cases connected to the family since 2008, says an earlier file recorded a diagnosis of a disorder that leads a caregiver to induce illness in their children, and that she warned of the risk. Prosecutors have not confirmed those points.

Sebastián Medina, head of Argentina's national ombudsman's office for children's rights, said the right of minors to be heard is a guiding principle of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and is not exhausted in a single procedural step. Where violence is suspected, he said, urgent protective measures should be taken and judicial and administrative proceedings coordinated. He said this case shows precisely the disconnect between criminal and family court files.

World.title: Two crew killed as firefighting helicopters collide in midair in Greece
World.content:
Two crew killed as firefighting helicopters collide in midair in Greece

2nd Sunday, August 2026 - 20:43 UTC Full article

A British pilot and a second Greek coordinator, aboard the other aircraft, survived with minor injuries and will remain in hospital for 24 hours under observation

Two crew members were killed on Sunday when two helicopters battling a wildfire collided in midair in the Psatha area, on the boundary between Attica and Boeotia northwest of Athens, the Hellenic Fire Service said.

The victims were a Danish pilot and a Greek fire service liaison officer. A British pilot and a second Greek coordinator, aboard the other aircraft, survived with minor injuries and will remain in hospital for 24 hours under observation. All four crew members were located after the crash; two were found unconscious and later pronounced dead. Their names have not been released.

Video recorded by a bystander shows one aircraft striking the rotor of the other, which caught fire and fell into a ravine. The second made an emergency landing in an area of low vegetation. According to the Ekathimerini website, the survivors immediately reported the collision and guided rescuers to the crash site.

Two Bell 214ST firefighting helicopters collided mid-air while battling a major forest fire in the Psatha area, west of Athens, Greece, triggering a search and rescue operation.



Aircraft involved: One helicopter was Bell 214ST N511EV (serial 28105, built in 1982), while… pic.twitter.com/Jwd3qpLAfj — FL360aero (@fl360aero) August 2, 2026

The two Bell helicopters were leased by the fire service from an Australian company, each carrying two crew. They had taken off from Elefsina military airport. In line with protocol, the country's entire Bell fleet has been grounded, a source at the civil protection ministry told the BBC. The same source said the British pilot was a private aviator hired for the wildfire season and was not part of any cooperation program between the United Kingdom and Greece.

The crash occurred in adverse weather. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said winds reached Force 10 on the Beaufort scale in several areas of the country. The gusts prevented water-bombing aircraft from collecting water from the sea, leaving helicopters as the only aerial assets able to operate. Mitsotakis expressed deep sorrow over the accident and sent condolences to the families. Three firefighters died in the line of duty on Wednesday.

The fire front was advancing on Sunday toward Megara and its industrial zone, with evacuation warnings issued through the 112 emergency system and police going door to door. Canadair aircraft, Chinook helicopters and Erickson Air-Crane units continue firefighting operations.

In France, the country's largest wildfire remains contained within a 420-square-kilometer perimeter, with hot spots still burning and nearly 3,000 firefighters deployed, alongside a second uncontained blaze in Provence. The evacuation of 224,000 people in the Gironde was among the largest in French civilian history.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, having warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the Copernicus climate service. An analysis by World Weather Attribution concluded that climate change made the extreme fire-weather conditions behind the French blazes at least twice as likely.

World.title: Lula pledges defense spending so no one invades Brazil as he confirms his candidacy
World.content:
Lula pledges defense spending so no one invades Brazil as he confirms his candidacy

2nd Sunday, August 2026 - 20:29 UTC Full article

He said he wants to be prepared so that no one invades the country to take away its president, as has happened elsewhere, adding that he wants to be prepared for peace, not for war

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pledged on Sunday to increase defense investment if he wins October's elections, as his re-election bid was formalized at the Workers' Party national convention held at the Expo Center Norte in São Paulo.

He said he wants to be prepared so that no one invades the country to take away its president, as has happened elsewhere, adding that he wants to be prepared for peace, not for war. The remark was an apparent reference to the capture of Nicolás Maduro by US special forces on January 3 in Caracas, though he did not name him.

Lula urged left-wing supporters to stop treating defense as a minor matter and cited the strengthening of military industries in the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan. He acknowledged reservations among part of the electorate stemming from the 1964-1985 military dictatorship, but argued the country must protect its more than 213 million inhabitants, 8.5 million square kilometers of territory and over 8,000 kilometers of coastline amid international instability. He had previously criticized NATO's increases in military spending.

The president also said he would address the exploitation of rare earths and critical minerals, and stated he would not allow interference from either China or the United States on the matter. He argued Brazil should use its own technological capacity to extract and process them, describing them as national patrimony. International estimates place the country among the world's largest holders of reserves, largely unexplored, behind China.

The convention proclaimed the ticket of Lula and Geraldo Alckmin, whose vice-presidential candidacy had been ratified days earlier by the PSB. The coalition brings together seven parties: PT, PSB, PSOL, Rede, PV, PCdoB and PDT. Party president Edinho Silva formalized the announcement.

The event was restrained in tone, with brief speeches designed for circulation on social media. Before speaking, Lula criticized the absence of women from the program and handed the microphone to First Lady Rosângela Lula da Silva, who promotes the national plan against femicide. Alckmin and São Paulo gubernatorial candidate Fernando Haddad also spoke.

At 80, Lula avoided direct references to his rivals and said his is the only candidacy that will not need to resort to lies during the campaign. He also made no mention of Donald Trump, whose tariff offensive has dominated the agenda in recent weeks, apart from one passing joke.

The formal campaign launch is scheduled for August 16 at the Vila Euclides stadium in São Bernardo do Campo. Polls give Lula a lead over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the main opposition candidate. On Thursday, the Supreme Federal Court authorized an investigation into the president's eldest son over alleged influence-peddling.

World.title: Bachelet places fourth in first Security Council straw poll ahead of Uruguay debate
World.content:
Bachelet places fourth in first Security Council straw poll ahead of Uruguay debate

2nd Sunday, August 2026 - 20:11 UTC Full article

Bachelet, 74, a former executive director of UN Women and former high commissioner for human rights, faces an unusual situation: her candidacy lacks the backing of her own country's government

Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet placed fourth in the Security Council's first informal poll on the candidates seeking to succeed António Guterres at the head of the United Nations, held behind closed doors in New York on Thursday.

According to figures attributed to diplomatic sources, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan led the round with ten encouraging votes, one against and four no-opinion ballots, followed by Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett with nine, two and four, and Argentina's Rafael Grossi with seven, five and three. Bachelet received six votes in favor, five against and four no-opinion. Behind her came Senegal's Macky Sall, Ecuador's María Fernanda Espinosa and Uganda's Olara Otunnu, who entered the race in recent days.

The outcome is formally secret. The Council's rotating president, Congolese Ambassador Zénon Mukongo Ngay, confirmed the poll had taken place without releasing figures, and how each of the fifteen members voted is not known. The straw polls are informal and non-binding, intended to test the viability of candidacies before the Council recommends a name to the General Assembly. Guterres's term ends on December 31.

Bachelet, 74, a former executive director of UN Women and former high commissioner for human rights, faces an unusual situation: her candidacy lacks the backing of her own country's government. It was presented in February by then-president Gabriel Boric together with the governments of Mexico and Brazil, but in March José Antonio Kast's administration withdrew its sponsorship, while pledging not to support any other contender.

The Chilean government argued that the chances of success were low given the number of Latin American candidacies and the lack of support among the five permanent members. The opposition attributed the decision to pressure from Washington, without providing evidence.

Brazil and Mexico maintained their support. Brazilian diplomatic sources said the candidacy is a priority for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. A group of former Chilean foreign ministers from across the political spectrum organized to advise Bachelet and arrange meetings with Council members. Heraldo Muñoz, foreign minister during her second term, said the sponsorship of both countries offsets the Chilean withdrawal and that Thursday's result was received calmly.

Academics consulted by EFE said there is no recent precedent for a case of this kind. The UN observes an unwritten regional rotation that would now fall to Latin America, and several states are calling for the post to go to a woman for the first time. According to EFE, the seven candidates debate on Monday in Uruguay.

World.title: Trump halts strikes on Iran as Tehran denies any deal exists
World.content:
Trump halts strikes on Iran as Tehran denies any deal exists

2nd Sunday, August 2026 - 20:00 UTC Full article

The announcement followed a phone call between Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman

US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he was suspending further strikes on Iran, saying the broad terms of an understanding had been agreed, an account Iranian authorities rejected hours later.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him to postpone any attack after the parameters of a deal were settled, one that would include the immediate, complete and total opening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the Iranian nuclear threat. He added that he agreed to cancel the operation provided a deal can be reached quickly, and said Israel was joining the commitment.

Tehran denied that account. The Fars news agency, affiliated with the Revolutionary Guard, described the announcement as another withdrawal of threats. People close to the Iranian negotiating team, quoted by domestic media, called the remarks a lie, denied any understanding on Hormuz and reiterated that the waterway will remain closed as long as Washington maintains what they term hostile actions. The acting defense minister said US statements would not confuse Iranian forces.

The announcement followed a phone call between Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. According to the official Saudi news agency, the prince stressed the need to prioritize dialogue to reduce regional tensions. Sources cited by the Associated Press and Axios said it was the prince who urged Trump to refrain from further strikes. Riyadh fears a US offensive against Iranian energy infrastructure could trigger retaliation on Saudi territory, at a time when the Houthis have announced a naval blockade on shipping from that country in the Red Sea.

Israel, which launched the offensive alongside the United States on February 28 but was not party to the June memorandum, is awaiting the outcome of the diplomatic effort. Its prime minister said options for continuing the campaign had been reviewed.

This is not the first such announcement. On March 23 Trump ordered strikes postponed for five days; on March 26 he extended an ultimatum; on April 7 he announced a two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan; and on June 17 a memorandum of understanding was signed opening sixty days of negotiations, which lapsed without effect.

Iran keeps Hormuz largely closed. Before the war, around 20% of the world's traded oil and liquefied natural gas passed through it, and the closure has pushed energy prices higher. On Saturday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO logged two incidents off the coast of Oman: a tanker struck by a projectile of unknown origin, damaging its engine room, and an explosion in the water alongside another vessel. There were no casualties.

Tehran puts the death toll since March at more than 3,400, a figure that has not been independently verified.

World.title: Argentina's central bank reform bill reaches the lower house: what would change
World.content:
Argentina's central bank reform bill reaches the lower house: what would change

31st Friday, July 2026 - 23:11 UTC Full article

The reform is part of a package that includes what the government calls the fiscal shackle

Argentina's executive branch sent the bill to overhaul the central bank's charter to the Chamber of Deputies on Friday, a day after President Javier Milei outlined it in a nationwide broadcast. The measure will formally enter the parliamentary record on Monday and be referred to committees; the government hopes to pass it in August.

The text is organized around six pillars. The first replaces article 3 of the current statute to establish that the institution's primary and fundamental mission is to preserve the value of the currency. It thereby supersedes the multiple mandate set in 2012, under Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, which included financial stability, employment and economic development with social equity. According to the bill's rationale, a central bank charged with everything cannot be held accountable for anything. The bill also strips the board of powers to channel credit toward small businesses and regional economies.

The second pillar sets specific grounds for removing board members, limited to serious and manifest failures arising from precise facts. Removal would require an executive decree with prior approval by both chambers, by a two-thirds majority of members present. It scraps the bicameral committee mechanism used in 2010, when the government sought to remove Martín Redrado as bank president, and eliminates the presence of an Economy Ministry representative at board meetings.

The third pillar bars all channels of financing to the public sector. It repeals temporary advances, prohibits loans to the national government, the provinces, the City of Buenos Aires and municipalities, bans purchases of government paper in the primary market and eliminates the freely available reserves established by the 1991 convertibility law. The executive's message states that the current administration could have transferred up to 36.6 trillion pesos to the Treasury through advances, more than 80% of the monetary base, and that non-transferable notes on the bank's books totaled 69.4 billion dollars as of April 2025.

The fourth pillar restricts profit distribution: only realized and liquid earnings not stemming from exchange rate movements or gold valuation could be transferred, reserves must reach at least 50% of the bank's capital, and any transfer must go toward cancelling public debt. The practice of remitting accounting gains from exchange rate differences to the Treasury has been used by every administration since convertibility ended, including the current one. The remaining pillars address balance sheet cleanup and update operational and reserve rules.

The reform is part of a package that includes what the government calls the fiscal shackle, a mechanism for partially shutting down state operations in the event of sustained deficits, along with capital markets and insurance sector reforms. Santiago Bausili's appointment as central bank president still lacks Senate confirmation.

World.title: Mexico Well-Read: A review of Reyna Grande’s ‘Migrant Heart’
World.content:
There is a particular unease that arises from hearing stories about crossing a border you have also crossed, but in the opposite direction and under radically better circumstances. I savored Reyna Grande’s new memoir, “Migrant Heart: Essays About Things I Can’t Forget,” in the comfort of my home in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, a gorgeous town famous for its architecture, arts scene, climate and ever-growing expat population. Grande’s life story began only a day’s drive but a world away, in Iguala, Guerrero — a town most of the world now knows, if they know it at all, as the place where 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Teachers’ College disappeared in 2014, an atrocity that still hangs over Mexican public life like an unfinished storm.

The book itself deserves to be met on its own considerable terms, because “Migrant Heart” is not a polemic. It is something much rarer and better: a mid-career writer’s attempt to loosen her grip on the story that made her famous. Grande’s earlier memoirs, “The Distance Between Us” and “A Dream Called Home,” shared the traumas of her childhood and young adulthood, and relayed them so devastatingly that a friend of the author’s once suggested, not entirely as a joke, that the publisher bundle a box of tissues with each copy.

Reyna Grande is the ‘queen of misery’ no more

In this new memoir-in-essays, Grande resists that role. She opens by recounting her experience of being crowned the “queen of misery,” and the whole book can be read as her working out what it might mean to put down that crown without abandoning the truths that earned it.

The 18 essays here range further afield than her previous work, into failing eyesight, gardening, motherhood, menopause and the peculiar vertigo of raising American children who will never fully understand her scars or carry her burdens. She writes about the Ayotzinapa disappearances not as distant news but as a wound in her hometown’s soul. She writes about losing fluency in Spanish as the price of gaining English, and about the complicated inheritance of colorism within Mexican and Mexican American communities — including, in one unsparing passage, her own mother’s hope that her grandchild would have blue eyes.

Grande has said in interviews that she has worried about repeating herself, about her writing calcifying into “immigrant trauma porn,” and in these essays you can feel her actively resisting that fate, reaching instead for the harder, less marketable material of an ordinary life continuing after the extraordinary parts are over. This is a writer who has spent two decades making readers weep; here, she seems more interested in proving she can let herself, as well as her readers, breathe.

In “Migrant Heart,” Grande again affirms that pain can be transformed into power. But she finally permits herself to set some careful boundaries, too, no longer feeling compelled to reexamine every wound for the reader’s benefit.

Not a comfortable read, but one filled with ‘hard truths’

For us expats reading this book in any of the beautiful, sunny Mexican towns that serve as havens for people fleeing not violence and brutal poverty but cold winters, polarized politics and high property taxes, “Migrant Heart” is not entirely comfortable reading, and I don’t think it should be. But it is essential reading precisely because our comfort here was built on a complicated history that these essays insist we look at directly. Living where I live, I could not read this without feeling implicated, gently but unmistakably, in the very economic and political inequities that produced both the author’s and my own radically different migrant experiences.

Grande has written a book about what it costs to leave home when you have no choice; the least those of us who have enjoyed that choice can do is read it all the way through and wrestle with some hard truths along the way.

Ann Marie Jackson is a book editor and the award-winning author of “The Broken Hummingbird.” She lives in San Miguel de Allende and can be reached through her website: annmariejacksonauthor.com.

World.title: How Jorge Campos won over the fans at the 2026 FIFA World Cup
World.content:
You don’t have to be a futbolero to know the national icon that is Jorge “El Inmortal” Campos.

The former Mexican national team goalkeeper, who stood a mere 5-foot-6, dominated throughout the 1990s as a stalwart between the goalposts, supplying acrobatic dives and theatrical saves that have been compiled into countless highlight reels by a zealous fanbase. On the field, he helped popularize the role of an attacking goalie — the rare archetype of a goalkeeper who would leave his own goal to become an offensive weapon against opposing defenses (Campos famously played striker at times, netting over 35 goals in his career).

In fact, Campos developed such a prolific and unprecedented style as an offensive-minded goalie that FIFA was prompted to investigate its own rules about a player who switches positions mid-game.

‘A cult hero for his flamboyant apparel’

From 1988 to 2004, Campos — who grew up near Acapulco, Guerrero — transformed into a larger-than-life force during his prime, playing in Mexico and the United States for teams like UNAM, Atlante, LA Galaxy, Cruz Azul, Chicago Fire, Tigres and Puebla.

But perhaps more than the game itself, Campos became a cult hero for his flamboyant apparel. Bright neon shades and quirky geometric designs highlighted his loud sense of fashion on the pitch and, decades later, he remains one of soccer’s most iconic global personalities. At his zenith, Campos designed his own kit (inspired by Acapulco’s culture) that he wore in the 1994 World Cup. Campos’ creativity inspired other goalkeepers of the decade to follow suit, as a few of his contemporaries would also go on to create their own flamboyant style modeled after his example.

In total, Campos is credited with 130 national appearances for Mexico and over 100 custom uniform designs. In his own words, “I’m not sure if I played that well, but everyone remembers me.” Indeed, they do.

This summer, Campos recaptured the hearts of soccer fans worldwide with his playful personality, generous spirit and the announcement of a new soccer endorsement deal with Nike — a rare feat for a long-retired veteran. Here’s how the immortal Campos further embellished his colorful legacy at the 2026 World Cup.

Nike’s ‘Campos x Jorge’ collection

In his biggest splash, Campos revealed his collaboration with Nike for the “Campos x Jorge” release. Though the exact dates of the drop haven’t been confirmed yet, the sportswear giant teased the clothing line throughout the World Cup. (A few months ago, Campos joined forces with Nike and the Houston rapper Travis Scott, who is a frequent Nike collaborator himself, to release a custom jersey under the BadFriend skate apparel brand, perhaps foreshadowing Campos’ own line.)

The clothing will utilize Campos’ legendary patterns, designs and colors. Best of all, Nike unveiled a Michael Jordan-esque silhouette for the brand, in which the outline of a diving Campos punching a ball away from the goalpost serves as a makeshift “Jumpman” logo.

Images of conceptual sketches have emerged online, generating tons of fan excitement around the clothing line. References to palm trees, Acapulco, beaches, surfing (a hobby that Campos acquired while growing up on Mexico’s Pacific coast) and, of course, soccer are at the forefront.

The collection will honor Campos’ ongoing tradition of converting the soccer field into a fashion runway.

Campos’ role as a cultural ambassador for Mexico

Nowadays, Campos is a versatile diplomat for the game’s universal appeal, a goalkeeper who transcended the sport to become an avatar of Mexico’s vibrancy and warmth beyond the penalty box.

For the 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted in his native Mexico, Campos was in a uniquely opportune position to represent the sport as an official FIFA World Cup ambassador — along with other soccer notables like David Beckham, Mia Hamm, Ronaldo Nazário and Ronaldinho Gaúcho. Throughout the Cup, Campos was seen inside VIP boxes and attending high-profile events in various host cities, rubbing shoulders with the biggest stars in the sport. He was even given a seat in the presidential box with FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

In addition, Campos served as a World Cup television commentator for Mexico’s Azteca Deportes, providing analysis of in-game action, which he has done for over 20 years since his retirement in the mid-2000s. He is known for being goofy, off the cuff and rather unserious — albeit sincere and endearing — in a way that brings levity to the commentator’s booth.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jorge Campos Navarrete (@soyjorgecampos1)

His face was seen everywhere, especially in Mexico: on limited-edition children’s juice boxes on Boing!, in Visa s and in television commercials alongside other Mexican celebrities like El Hijo del Santo, Julio César Chávez and Pedro Infante.

‘A meeting of legends’

Beyond the gimmicky commercialism of it all, which admittedly has become an increasingly diluted part of the sporting industry at large in the modern age, Campos helped bring unity across cultures and generations in genuine, organic ways.

Most memorably, Campos brought René “El Loco” Higuita — a famous Colombian goalie from the 1990s known for his daredevil saves and infamous “scorpion kick” — together with Vozinha, who became Cape Verde’s unlikely goalkeeping hero and was considered the fan-favorite goalkeeper of this 2026 tournament. (Vozinha blocked all of Spain’s shot attempts and shut down the eventual World Cup champions with a 0-0 draw in their group stage duel.)

Jorge Campos and the 2026 FIFA World Cup

In a now-viral video, Campos asks Higuita, “Who is the best keeper?” to which Higuita responds, “Jorge Campos.” Campos immediately corrects him with a smile and says, “No, Vozinha,” and calls Vozinha over from across the room, whom Higuita hadn’t yet seen. The trio takes a photo together in a cross-generational meeting of legends. Later, Campos and Vozinha exchanged jerseys, a tradition that represents a sign of mutual respect and admiration between high-caliber players. Campos ends the interaction by telling them all to say “hello to Mexico.”

In Mexico, you can’t mention the 2026 World Cup without mentioning Jorge Campos. And you can’t mention Campos without mentioning Mexico.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: When Mexico colonized California
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico covers 1.96 million square kilometers (about 757,000 square miles), making it the 13th-largest country in the world. It once stretched over a far greater area and included six modern U.S. states, including the vast forests, mountains and deserts of California. To understand how Mexico occupied the West Coast of North America, we need to understand the geography of the continent.

The Atlantic coastline of what is now the United States was colonized by Britain and seemed to offer little other than farmland. In the southern half of the continent, the Amazon restricted colonization to the coast. European expansion, led by the Spanish, therefore funneled through the Caribbean Islands, where the climate was suited for plantations, and into Central America, where there was the promise of gold and other riches. Mexico — or “New Spain” as it was known for three centuries — was not only a vast country, but the center of a great Spanish empire that at its height stretched for some 11,000 kilometers (about 6,800 miles) from the tip of Argentina almost to the edge of Alaska.

Spanish shipbuilding in Mexico

Cortés brought down the Mexica empire in 1521, and although Spanish exploration did not stop, it slowed down. One problem was the lack of ships on the Pacific coast, for rounding Cape Horn was a dangerous venture for any captain. However, once the Spanish were established in Central America, ships could be dismantled, hauled across the isthmus, and reassembled. The establishment of the shipyards required for such work first centered on the Gulf of San Miguel in modern Panama, where it was just 60 kilometers (about 37 miles) from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The initial driving force for such activity was not the old dream of exploration, but the need to transport enslaved peoples from Central America to the new mines opening up in Peru.

Such ships were generally caravels, 40 to 75 feet in length and weighing between 50 and 160 tons. Their small size and frame-first design meant a ship could be assembled in three to nine months, and within a decade, modest shipbuilding enterprises had sprung up in numerous places along the coast. These included Acapulco, where Hernán Cortés encouraged the industry with the building of a wharf and the marking out of a rough road to Mexico City.

Explorations of California

Not that exploration stopped altogether, and as early as 1533, Hernán Cortés sent a small party to investigate California, whose name came from a 1510 Spanish romance novel by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo, “Las Sergas de Esplandián.” They did not find that elusive route to China, nor the rumored “seven cities of gold,” but Fortún Jiménez became the first European to set foot on Baja California.

Cortés himself arrived in what is now La Paz in May 1535. He believed Baja to be an island, which he claimed for Spain. There was no gold, but there were pearl beds, and a small colony was founded. However, the terrain and climate proved too harsh, and this first settlement was abandoned. In 1539, Francisco de Ulloa sailed north on a new mission of exploration, and he discovered that Baja was not an island but a peninsula. The letter he sent back to Acapulco did not encourage others to follow. The land, he declared, was “ugly and barren, as poor here as it was in parts seen earlier.”

The Manila-Acapulco galleon trade

Shipbuilding was making great strides on the Pacific coast, and by 1542, two expeditions could be dispatched. Ruy López de Villalobos sailed with six Guatemalan-built ships to head for the Philippines, while Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sailed with three ships to explore the “uncharted waters of the north.” The Cabrillo fleet sailed past Baja to California proper, perhaps reaching as far as the mouth of the Russian River that lies well north of modern San Francisco. Cabrillo did not survive the journey. He slipped on some rocks and shattered his shin, a wound that became infected with gangrene. He died on Jan. 3, 1543.

A few concessions were handed out for the exploitation of the pearl beds within the Gulf of California, and there were souls to be saved, which motivated the opening of a handful of small missions in the southern half of the peninsula. However, little interest was shown in the lands beyond the peninsula. What drew the Spanish back to these waters was the opening of the trade route with the Philippines.

Why the galleons sailed down the California Coast

This had taken time to establish, for while sailing to the Philippines was a harsh journey, it was also relatively straightforward. Winds and currents made the return journey far more complex, and it was 1565 before the Spanish discovered that by sailing north to around 40 degrees of latitude, a ship could pick up the westerly trade winds and benefit from the powerful Kuroshio Current. Even if all went well, reaching the American coast could take months, and ships would strike land far to the north. Returning galleons now sailed down the California coast each year, and no doubt knowledge of this unexplored world was passed on by word of mouth, but we have no record of such conversations.

Pirates and explorers

Another wanderer along the Pacific coast was not Spanish but the English hero — or pirate, depending on your point of view — Francis Drake. He left Plymouth in 1577 and reached the Strait of Magellan in September 1578. He headed into this strait with six ships, but only the Golden Hind survived the notorious storms that ravaged these waters. After terrorizing the Spanish coast, he sailed north beyond Spanish reach, where he stopped to repair his ship and claim the land for England. His precise landing point is uncertain, but it would have been north of modern San Francisco. From here, Drake headed out into the Pacific to complete the first circumnavigation of the globe in 58 years.

There was another motivation for exploring along the California coast: the search for the Strait of Anian. This northern passage to the Atlantic started to appear on maps from around 1560, but its existence had never been confirmed. In 1584, Franciscus Gaill continued the exploration of the Pacific coast, describing California in promising terms and noting the abundance of seals. The record of his journey might have been lost to us except that an account somehow found its way into the travel journals of the Dutch explorer Jan Huygen.

Cavendish and the taking of the Manila galleon

The English had not gone away, and in 1587 the privateer Thomas Cavendish lurked off the coast of Baja California, where he seized and burned the Manila galleon Santa Ana. The crew was put ashore with supplies and survived, with two of the officers, Vizcaíno and Cermeño, going on to become important explorers of this coast. In 1595, Sebastián Rodríguez Cermeño commanded the Manila galleon San Agustín with orders to explore the California coastline on the return journey. He was anchored in a small bay when they were hit by a storm that sank his great ship. Cermeño and his crew struggled home in a small boat, but the loss of the Manila galleon must have been a devastating blow to the Spanish economy that year.

A search for a safe harbor

This loss demonstrated the need for a safe harbor along the Northern coast, and in 1601, the search was entrusted to Sebastián Vizcaíno. He was well acquainted with these waters, having sailed on the Manila galleons himself and having also operated pearl concessions from La Paz. Vizcaíno mapped the California coastline as far north as Monterey without finding a suitable harbor. He felt Monterey Bay was unsuitable as it was exposed to rough currents and winds, and he missed San Francisco Bay completely, most likely passing when it was shrouded in mist.

There was no obvious harbor, little promise from the land and the British threat seemed to have passed. Spanish interest faded with the world beyond the Baja California peninsula, and ships returning from the Philippines were left to find shelter and take on water where they could. This period of apathy would last a century and a half.

José de Gálvez and the founding of new missions in California

In 1765, José de Gálvez arrived in New Spain as the king’s special deputy. The Spanish government was bankrupt after the Seven Years’ War, and New Spain would have to refill the royal coffers. The ambitious Gálvez imposed state monopolies and introduced new taxes. Playing on fears that the British, Dutch or even the Russians had ambitions for the northern Pacific coast, he prepared a grand expedition that would not just explore, but would colonize the north.

Don Gaspar de Portolá, a Spanish Army officer from minor Catalan nobility, was given command of the land expedition, and with him would be the remarkable Father Junípero Serra. He was a member of the Franciscan Order and, on arriving in New Spain in 1749, had refused the offer of a horse and walked to Mexico City. He arrived with his left foot swollen and infected, a painful condition that remained with him the rest of his life.

The journey of Serra and Portolá

Gaspar de Portolá’s overland party reached the site of present-day San Diego in July 1769 to find that the two galleons carrying their supplies had only just arrived. They had missed the bay and sailed lost for several weeks, during which time the crews were devastated by scurvy. The initial force of 300 men was down to half that number, but Portolá continued northward with 63 soldiers and 100 mules. Moving painfully slowly, they arrived in what is now Los Angeles in early August. Early November saw them cross a low coastal mountain range and look down on San Francisco Bay, the perfect harbor that the Spanish had been seeking for so long.

Back in San Diego, Father Serra built a small hut to act as a church, and this would grow into the Mission San Diego. During the early years, this and the other missions that followed would be dependent on supply ships arriving from Mexico, but a local economy was slowly established, based around raising cattle.

California (California and Baja California weren’t formally recognized as separate territories until 1804), however, remained a neglected outpost of a faltering Spanish empire, with the Spanish population never rising above 14,000. Within three decades, Lewis and Clark would complete the first east-to-west crossing of the northern half of the continent, bringing the Pacific Coast within the sights of the small but ambitious and rapidly expanding United States of America.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Conjoined twins dominate synchronized swimming event in Mexico
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

Following a dominant gold-medal performance at the World Watersports Championships, international sports officials confirmed Tuesday that Mexico’s premier synchronized diving team has officially cleared all regulations for competitive fairness, provided they continue using the same shared torso.

Fourteen-year-old prodigies Sofia and Valentina Gómez secured the top spot during the synchronized final over the world-ranked team from China. The victory marked the first time a Mexican team defeated the top-seeded international pair, a feat sports analysts attribute to flawless execution, rigorous daily preparation and an absolute physical inability to desynchronize mid-air.

World Watersports adjudicators spent three hours reviewing high-speed footage of the final dive to determine whether the pair’s shared center of gravity provided an unfair mechanical advantage. The panel ultimately ruled that while perfect temporal alignment is guaranteed, the pair faces unique structural handicaps, including a single assigned locker and the logistical challenge of fitting two regulation warm-up robes over one set of shoulders.

“The rules state that synchronized partners must initiate rotation at the exact same millisecond,” said World Watersports technical delegate Jean-Luc Moreau. “Normally, achieving that level of timing requires a decade of joint training and agonizing repetition. The Gómez twins have achieved it through cellular-level integration. It is unusual, but entirely within the parameters of the rulebook.”

The victory has sparked intense interest among international coaching staff, who have traditionally relied on verbal cues and mirrored drill repetitions to build symmetry. Team officials confirmed that while rival nations have already inquired about training techniques, the pair’s success relies on a highly specialized regimen consisting primarily of mutual agreement on which direction to turn when leaving the locker room.

“We felt very happy with the result,” said Sofia Gómez during the post-event press conference, speaking simultaneously with her sister without looking in her direction. “It gives us a lot of motivation for the upcoming Olympics, where we hope to show that perfect harmony is not just about communication, but about literally sharing a circulatory system.”

Sports bioengineers noted that the pair’s springboard entry achieved an entry angle deviation of 0.00 degrees, a statistic never before recorded in international competition. Analysts added that while traditional synchronized pairs spend years managing interpersonal friction, the Gómez twins have effectively eliminated all miscommunication by operating off a single central nervous system.

The pair is slated to represent Mexico at the upcoming 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, where event organizers confirmed they will be issued two gold medals, but only a single set of accreditation credentials.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Authorities capture CJNG leader, Navy backs US $115M sargassum strategy and Kia commits $649M to EVs
World.content:
The week of July 27th in Mexico ended with a major security win as agents captured the alleged intellectual author of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s assassination, a case that rattled Michoacán, a state burdened by organized crime, in late 2025.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, meanwhile, spent much of the week swatting away rhetorical grenades lobbed from abroad: she rejected Argentine President Javier Milei’s claim that Mexico was funding an “anti-Argentina campaign,” and brushed off White House adviser Stephen Miller’s assertion that cartels control Mexico’s political system, telling reporters the United States “must look at itself” on drug consumption. Closer to home, a cheating scandal consumed Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university, which confronted suspicions that AI and old-fashioned cheat sheets had corrupted its admissions exam. In a lighter moment, chefs in the capital’s Venustiano Carranza borough assembled a 100-meter, 1.5-tonne torta at the International Torta Fair, a Guinness-certified spectacle that drew hundreds of thousands of visitors.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mastermind of Manzo murder captured in Jalisco

Federal authorities on Thursday arrested Ramón Ángel “R1” Álvarez Ayala, the alleged mastermind behind the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Álvarez Ayala, leader of a CJNG-linked cell known as “Los R’s,” was apprehended in Atotonilco, Jalisco, in an operation involving a high-speed chase and a shootout that left one of his bodyguards dead. García Harfuch later detailed R1’s criminal history, noting he was first jailed in 2012 for orchestrating a wave of violence in Guadalajara, was released in 2022, and resumed criminal activity soon after — allegedly ordering several killings, including that of influencer Valeria Márquez. His capture marks the 31st arrest connected to Manzo’s murder, a killing that shocked Mexico’s political and business classes and turned the independent mayor into a national symbol of local officials’ vulnerability to organized crime.

Mexicans now view China more favorably than the US, Pew finds

A new Pew Research Center survey found that Mexicans view China more favorably than the United States for the first time in nearly two decades of polling. Some 59% of Mexican respondents said they had a favorable opinion of China, compared to 40% for the U.S., and Mexicans were roughly three times more likely to express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping than in Donald Trump. Canada showed a similar reversal, and Pew noted the trend held across most of the 36 countries it surveyed. Analysts attribute the shift largely to worsening views of Washington rather than improving perceptions of Beijing, with younger Mexican adults especially likely to favor China over the U.S.

Chemical spill near Arizona border triggers emergency response

Two separate freight train derailments prompted emergency responses over the weekend. In Ciudad Madero, Tamaulipas, authorities declared a Code Red and evacuated more than 200 residents after a Pemex-owned tank car carrying 70,000 liters of gasoline tipped over in a rail yard.

Farther north, a Ferromex freight train derailed in Naco, Sonora, spilling roughly 59,000 liters of sodium hydrosulfide, a corrosive chemical used in copper mining, just south of the U.S. border. Heavy rain then hampered cleanup efforts in Sonora, forcing families near the Cuauhtémoc ejido to temporarily leave their homes due to fumes. Sonora’s Civil Protection Agency said emergency measures were deployed immediately, while the National Water Commission is testing water and soil to determine whether the chemical reached waterways near Cananea. The Federal Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation into the derailment, which occurred on a Grupo México-linked rail line and raised fresh concerns about industrial safety in a state that is already home to some of Mexico’s largest copper mining operations.

Del Toro caps historic Tour de France

Cyclist Isaac del Toro delivered Mexico’s best-ever Tour de France result, finishing third overall and taking the white jersey as the race’s best young rider — a result celebrated by President Sheinbaum. The 22-year-old from Ensenada, Baja California, made history early in the three-week race too, winning Stage 2 in Barcelona after teammate and four-time champion Tadej Pogačar eased up in the final meters to let the young rider take the victory, a gesture that left Del Toro visibly stunned. It was the first Tour stage win by a Mexican rider in 36 years, since Raúl Alcalá’s back-to-back victories in 1989 and 1990. Del Toro’s final-week performance in the Alps, where Pogačar again worked to protect his young teammate’s position, sealed a podium finish that surpassed Alcalá’s previous best of eighth place, cementing Del Toro’s status as Mexico’s greatest cyclist and a genuine contender for future Grand Tours.

Acapulco hydroelectric dam project scrapped

Sheinbaum canceled the long-controversial La Parota dam project near Acapulco, citing unresolved land expropriation issues and a lack of community agreements. In its place, the government will build radial wells along the Papagayo River, rehabilitate aqueducts and replace drinking water lines serving the city’s upper neighborhoods.

Foreign investment keeps flowing

Several new investment announcements underscored continued foreign interest in Mexico.

Houston-based Talos Energy agreed to acquire a 50% stake in Repsol’s offshore Block 29 in the Gulf of Mexico, home to the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries.

South Korean automaker Kia announced a US $649 million investment to begin producing its EV3 electric SUV at its Pesquería, Nuevo León plant starting Aug. 4 — the model’s first production site outside South Korea, expected to create 500 jobs this year and 1,500 more by 2030.

On the consumer side, U.S. cookie chain Crumbl opened its first Mexico store in Roma Norte, CDMX, to 800-person lines, while gourmet hot dog chain Dog Haus debuted in Mérida, part of a broader wave of American food brands expanding south.

Mexican economy shows signs of life

The MND Economy Index™, a 10-pillar composite gauge of Mexico’s economic health, rose to 68.61 in its latest edition — its highest reading yet, driven by improving inflation and monetary policy scores even as economic growth remains the weakest-performing pillar. The improving picture was reinforced by other data this week:

Mexico’s export revenue hit a record US $389.72 billion in the first half of 2026, a 24.6% annual increase driven by a surge in non-automotive manufacturing exports.

The economy grew 1.5% quarter-over-quarter in Q2, Mexico’s best result since late 2020, aided by World Cup-related tourism spending.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard also weighed in on the trade relationship with Washington, downplaying Trump’s latest remark that he “doesn’t care” about the USMCA. “Obviously there are warnings every week, there are a lot of things,” Ebrard told reporters, adding that “as of today we’re doing well.” Sheinbaum echoed the sentiment, noting the two countries’ economies remain deeply integrated after decades of free trade.

Navy presents US $115M sargassum plan

With Quintana Roo facing its worst sargassum season on record, the Mexican Navy announced a 2-billion-peso plan to combat the seaweed influx choking Caribbean coast beaches. The strategy includes roughly 50 kilometers of new anti-sargassum sea barriers near Playa del Carmen, Cancún, Tulum, Puerto Morelos and Mahahual, along with new collection vessels aimed at eventually processing 4,000 tonnes of sargassum per day. Quintana Roo has already collected more than 92,000 tonnes of the macroalgae this year, with officials projecting the total could exceed 119,000 tonnes before year’s end.

World Bank aligns support with Plan México

World Bank Group President Ajay Banga made his first visit to Mexico in five years, meeting with Sheinbaum to align a new five-year Country Partnership Framework with the government’s Plan México industrial strategy. The framework will prioritize infrastructure, energy, water management and human capital development.

Banga also toured Grupo Naturasol, a family-owned agribusiness in México state that previously received International Finance Corporation financing, calling it a model for how smaller firms can plug into North American supply chains.

World.title: When legacy media’s hypocrisy gets called out: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am increasingly finding myself analyzing the Mexico narrative as it’s told by different media outlets. Just this past week brought us another ludicrous example with The Atlantic magazine publishing an article titled “A Planeload of Informants” with the subtitle: “The United States is intensifying its hunt for narcos within the Mexican government. Is this all prelude to an attack?”

I guess The Atlantic was feeling left out of the party by other large media outlets writing breathtakingly sensationalist articles about Mexico. If you remember, leading up to the World Cup, The Economist magazine informed its readers that: “The World Cup will test Mexico’s control over its territory.” The Wall Street Journal told us that the “World Cup puts Mexico’s Cartel Crisis on the Global Stage.” And the New York Times has written at length of experts confidently predicting Mexico would enter a period of increasing violence after the February government operation against CJNG leader Mencho.

But they have all been wrong. Totally wrong. The post-Mencho spiral of violence? It didn’t happen. In fact, Mexico has seen its homicide rates hitting lows not seen in over a decade. The “World Cup test” of Mexico against the cartels? There was no test. The world watched with envy as foreigners partied alongside Mexicans across the country. Not a single article has been written acknowledging getting things so wrong. And so now we have the media moving on to the next big story: A potential attack by the United States on Mexico.

Let’s be clear about the history here: Mexico has, for decades, genuinely struggled with cartel violence, and I am not arguing otherwise. But what these outlets consistently omit is the context of the last year. Cooperation between the U.S. and Mexico against cartels is, in the words of officials on both sides, at unprecedented levels — a shift I’ve tracked in real time (see my columns on the World Cup coverage and Mexico’s business community). The result of that cooperation isn’t more violence; it’s homicides down by almost 50% this year. Apparently good news doesn’t sell subscriptions.

Which brings me to two personal anecdotes from this past week that I want to share:

Cancelling a 30-year subscription

The first took place at a friend’s dinner party in Mexico City. A few hours into some good conversation, he (quite randomly) asked me: “Do you still read The Economist magazine?” To which I responded that I do. He then said: “I have been a loyal subscriber for over 30 years, but I am about to cancel it. I am done with them.” His reasoning was enlightening: “I am tired of the narrative of their coverage. By cancelling my subscription with them, I am choosing to not pay attention to the reality that they are presenting.” He went on: “The predictive power of their writers and editors has changed … and as a result they are just flat out wrong on many topics.”

The words stuck with me as I have been increasingly feeling the same about The Economist. In just the past few months, I have actually written twice about how intellectually lazy, disingenuous and downright wrong their coverage has been regarding Mexico. Increasingly, as I read their coverage on the country, I have found myself wondering, “Why am I reading this? It’s not accurate. It’s sensationalist. And it doesn’t represent reality. Why am I paying to read something that I think is just plain wrong?”

As my friend’s cancellation shows, his decision reflects a broader pattern I’m seeing: As irresponsible coverage piles up, readers simply stop trusting — and stop paying for — outlets they once considered essential.

The conversation went further with others at the party explaining that, in contrast, they read Mexico News Daily precisely because it “provides optimism by showing me the Mexico that I want to believe exists today and believe can exist in the future.” The comment wasn’t made out of ignorance or a lack of information, but rather in a way that reinforced the optimism they have for Mexico. Said differently, they are choosing to align with a narrative of informed optimism versus colonialist click-bait pessimism. It’s unfortunate to increasingly see people tuning out of legacy media, but it’s easy to understand why they are doing it. As many outlets increasingly present a pessimistic, dystopian, doom-and-gloom view of much of the world — one that increasingly is out of touch with reality — many people are choosing to tune out.

The Economist’s Elon Musk interview

The second anecdote came earlier this week when I watched The Economist’s editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes, interview Tesla/SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The nearly 90-minute-long interview went on fine for the first hour, but then turned decidedly testy. Ms. Beddoes at one point begins to take issue with Musk’s assessment of the current state of the U.K. (where The Economist is based and where she lives). She questioned his motives, repeatedly said he was incorrect, accused him of supporting “fringe” and “far right” parties and questioned when he had last visited the U.K. To be clear, the point here is not whether Musk’s take on the U.K. is right or wrong, that’s a separate debate entirely.

Here you have the head of The Economist, the British publication that has increasingly misconstrued, misrepresented and irresponsibly presented other countries around the world, getting extremely defensive about someone questioning the U.K. She repeatedly took offense to any of Musk’s critiques of her own country, claiming “People say that you’re racist,” “people loathe you,” “What is the motivation for [participating in tribalism]?” It was quite shocking to see the head of a publication that for decades has portrayed much of the rest of the world as dangerous, backwards and corrupt take so much offense to someone questioning the current state and future direction of her own country.

As she waged increasingly personal attacks against Musk, he finally had enough and responded with a dagger: “A lot more people hate you, the media — more than you realize. Do you realize the media is despised? Do you realize … the favorable view of journalists is like 15%? … They hate you.” It was a striking moment. Her defensiveness made her and her publication feel small, out of touch, aloof. It was a moment where I found myself even further questioning the true motives of The Economist.

Musk’s jab about journalism’s approval rating isn’t just a soundbite — it’s the direct consequence of the pattern I described above. When outlets choose sensationalism over accuracy, they erode trust in journalism broadly, pushing people toward sources — credible or not — that at least feel honest to them.

Is The Economist really trying to live by its founding mission from 179 years ago of taking part “in a severe contest between intelligence, which presses forward, and an unworthy, timid ignorance obstructing our progress”? Or are they more likely contributing to the obstruction of progress with increasingly ignorant and biased journalism? If the latter is in fact the case, as I sadly suspect it is, they will likely experience more people like my friend moving on.

I strongly believe that the role of the media is more important than ever. But we in the media also needs to work harder than ever to earn your trust and respect — and many outlets seem to have forgotten that.

Thank you for reading and supporting MND.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Romería Closes With Zero Deaths and 1,772 Medical Cases
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Romería closed without a single reported death, ending a nine-day emergency operation in which the Costa Rican Red Cross treated 1,772 people along the roads into Cartago and moved 34 of them to hospitals. The count covers July 25 through August 2, the feast day of the Virgen de los Ángeles, and it climbed steadily through the final Sunday.

At midday the Red Cross reported 1,681 people treated — 1,477 medical cases, 164 trauma injuries and three burns — with 31 transfers to medical centers, of which 20 were classified urgent, six critical and five stable. The 1,772 figure released Sunday evening is the most recent tally and remains provisional until the institution issues its close-out report.

Milena Bogantes, regional operational sub-coordinator for the Red Cross, reviewed the pattern of cases as the operation wound down. Before the walking began, the organization had said the emergencies it sees most often on this route are heat-related illness and blood pressure episodes, and it had asked pilgrims to hydrate, wear broken-in shoes and reflective clothing, and carry any prescription medication with them. In the earliest cuts of the operation, most patients were over 40, with the single largest group aged 61 and up.

The scale of the response is hard to overstate. The Red Cross fielded more than 850 responders and over 145 emergency vehicles across eight aid stations strung between San Pedro, on the eastern edge of San José, and the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles. The busiest posts were at the basilica itself, at Ochomogo and at La Galera, with smaller volumes recorded at El Cristo, Conventillos and San Pedro.

Raúl Rivera Bonilla, director general of the Fuerza Pública, said officers seized small quantities of drugs and weapons over the course of the operation. Around 500 officers were assigned to the corridor from La Sabana to Cartago during the heaviest days, working alongside roughly 150 Traffic Police officers, municipal police units and a network of surveillance cameras along the route. Authorities have not announced charges arising from the seizures, and the Fuerza Pública said it would keep its deployment in place through Monday.

Mario Redondo, the mayor of Cartago, said municipal crews recovered 13 dogs found abandoned along the pilgrimage route and took them to the city’s animal care center, where they will receive veterinary attention and, where appropriate, be neutered. Redondo put the total municipal and interinstitutional deployment at roughly 3,000 people across police forces, the Red Cross and sanitation crews, and said they collected more than 34 metric tons (37 short tons) of solid waste.

The pilgrimage itself is a walk of about 22 kilometers (14 miles) from central San José to Cartago, though many people set out from far greater distances and walk for days. Church estimates put participation across the period at close to two million, and this year’s program carried additional weight as the centenary of the Virgin’s pontifical coronation, granted by Pope Pius XI in April 1926. The 2025 operation, by comparison, ended with 2,196 people treated, 47 transferred to medical centers and no deaths.

The observance is not quite finished. The traditional Pasada takes place Monday at 9 a.m., when the image of the Virgin is carried from the basilica to the Catedral Nuestra Señora del Carmen through streets covered in flower and sawdust carpets, accompanied by bands, mascaradas, oxcarts and boyeros. Roads through central Cartago close for the procession, and nine schools along the route switched to at-home learning for the day, returning to classrooms Tuesday. Anyone driving through the Cartago canton center Monday morning should expect closures and delays until the procession finishes and traffic is restored.

Since Costa Rica has just over five million people, moving a crowd on that scale along public highways for nine days and finishing with no fatalities is the number the institutions involved will point to. The operation has been refined over decades of repetition, and the outcome reflects that: the traffic plan staged months in advance, aid posts placed where the walking gets hardest, and thousands of volunteers standing on the shoulder of a highway at three in the morning handing out water.

World.title: Costa Rica Under Yellow Alert as Saturated Ground Raises Flood Risk
World.content:
If you are driving to Limón, Turrialba or the southern Pacific today, expect delays and check the road before you leave. A yellow alert is in effect today for Pococí, Guácimo, Siquirres, Matina and Turrialba after a tropical wave moved across overnight and a green alert covers a much wider stretch of the Caribbean, the Northern Zone and the south.

The green alert is for Limón and Talamanca on the Caribbean side, Sarapiquí, San Carlos, Río Cuarto, Los Chiles, Guatuso and Upala in the Northern Zone, and Pérez Zeledón, Buenos Aires, Osa, Golfito, Puerto Jiménez, Corredores and Coto Brus in the south. As a reminder. yellow means preparation and active monitoring, not evacuation. Green means stay aware and watch conditions where you are.

The reason the alert level went up has less to do with how much rain is coming than with how much has already fallen. Some watersheds are more than 90% saturated, which means the ground cannot absorb anything more. Rain that would normally soak in now runs straight off hillsides and into rivers that are already high. That is why a moderate downpour today can cause more damage than a heavier one would have caused two weeks ago.

Tropical Wave 28 crossed this morning and strengthened the band of storms sitting over the Pacific near Costa Rica. Rain arrived overnight near both coasts and across the Caribbean and Northern Zone lowlands. Through the afternoon, expect scattered moderate rain and thunderstorms along the Pacific coast and in the mountains west of the Central Valley, with more isolated showers over the northern and Caribbean plains. By evening the rain shifts toward the southern Pacific coast.

Totals should land between 20 and 40 millimeters (roughly 0.8 to 1.6 inches), with the heaviest accumulations reaching about 100 millimeters (roughly 4 inches) in the south. Isolated gusts near storm cells could hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour), enough to bring down branches and power lines.

Parts of the Caribbean, unfortunately, did not wait for today’s system. Flooding over the weekend affected Matina, Siquirres, Talamanca and Turrialba, and rescue crews worked before dawn Sunday in Matina, where a river overflow at Finca Estrada left 22 people cut off. Emergency teams are also watching Hamburgo, Islona and Dos Bocas, and the Sixaola river in Talamanca has been running high.

As we have suggested in previous articles when tropical waves come, do not drive through standing water, because you cannot see whether the road under it has washed out, and moving water only 30 centimeters (about a foot) deep can push a car sideways. Do not try to cross a swollen river or creek on foot for the same reason. In towns, storm drains that are already full will back up quickly, so streets can flood faster than the rain seems to justify. If you hear thunder, get inside and stay away from windows and tall isolated trees until it passes.

One more thing worth mentioning here, emergency lines fill up fast during weather events, and every call that is not an emergency delays one that is. Call 911 if someone is in danger.
